articles.title: Moment Margaret Hamilton receives presidential medal of honour
articles.summary: Barack Obama awarded the Apollo 11 software engineer with the America's highest civilian honour in 2016.
articles.body:
The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.

Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".

And in 2016, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Honor - the nation's highest civilian honour - by Barack Obama in a ceremony at the White House.

"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement announcing Hamilton's passing, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.

articles.title: The tech-broification of American science has officially begun
articles.summary: ﻿Trump’s ‘Golden Age’ of American science starts with dismantling it, while funneling billions into AI.
articles.body: The Trump administration unveiled the first “Genesis Mission” grants on Thursday, directing $5 billion toward hundreds of AI-driven science projects in an effort the White House has described as “comparable in urgency and ambition to the Manhattan Project.” At roughly the same time, Trump’s science adviser Michael Kratsios was on Capitol Hill selling lawmakers on an equally grandiose promise: “A New Golden Age” of American science, one that would prioritize artificial intelligence, robotics, and nuclear energy and downplay life sciences. Taken together, the two announcements offer the clearest picture yet of how Donald Trump wants to remake American science. They mark the latest front in a wider war on the research establishment — one that has worked to suppress “woke” or DEI projects, threatened funding for universities, researchers, and projects on ideological grounds, curtailed the flow of international students and researchers, and handed unprecedented control over federal funding to political appointees. The result has been the gradual, systemic dismantling of the long-established norms and institutions that, for all their flaws, helped turn the United States into the world’s scientific superpower. Researchers say the vision is ill-conceived, contradictory, and less a blueprint for scientific renewal than a politicized power grab that fundamentally misunderstands how science works. It treats public research more like a Silicon Valley startup than a public good, privileging measurable returns and speed over the slow, uncertain, and unpredictable work that has produced some of history’s most consequential discoveries. Far from reviving US science, they warn, the agenda could prove disastrous for American research. The Genesis Mission grants span fields ranging from drug discovery and biomedical science to energy, advanced materials, and robotics. The 278 projects, reportedly selected from over 5,000 applications, all share a common premise: leveraging AI to accelerate scientific discovery. The Energy Department, which led this round of funding, said the project will unite national laboratories, industry, and academia to pursue “breakthroughs in energy dominance, discovery science, and national security.” Technology companies including Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI are also contributing millions of dollars in compute, AI credits, and other support to the initiative. Kratsios explicitly linked the program to the administration’s broader science agenda, calling Genesis Mission “the culmination of the reforms suggested in” its “Golden Age” manifesto. Styled as a modern successor to Vannevar Bush’s 1945 policy report “Science, the Endless Frontier,” which shaped much of the postwar system of federal research funding, the lengthy document proposes shifting support away from institutions and toward individual scientists, while giving private companies a larger role in directing and conducting research, and political appointees more power to block grants they disagree with. AI features heavily, both as a tool for scientists and as an engine for discovery itself, and Kratsios encouraged government funds to increasingly go to AI use and individual researchers, rather than universities, traditional hubs of scholarship and research. More broadly, the manifesto favors a goal-oriented and results-driven approach that resembles a Silicon Valley startup more than traditional scientific enterprise. Venture capital and startup culture are built around identifying promising people, projects, and ideas, setting clear goals with measurable targets, and moving quickly, iterating constantly, and cutting work that seems unlikely to deliver results. Science operates differently. Basic research can take years or decades before its importance or practical implications become apparent and it requires a system capable of supporting work of uncertain, even seemingly dubious, value. Its outcomes cannot always be predicted, and some of the most important discoveries emerge serendipitously from research pursuing entirely different questions. A science funding system needs to account for those differences, said Claes de Vreese, a professor of AI and society at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands. “You cannot use venture capital to force breakthroughs while virtually already selling the patent.” That model also stands in stark contrast to Bush’s championing of open-ended basic research pursued without an eye for immediate dividends, on the grounds that such work would ultimately yield applied breakthroughs. The scientific system built around that principle is what helped turn the United States into the world’s research superpower. Even so, it is not the first time the Trump administration has invoked Bush’s legacy to sell policies that would dismantle the system he helped create. Some of its proposals have obvious appeal, including reducing the administrative burdens on scientists, speeding up grantmaking, and making the system more flexible. Jason Shepherd, a professor of neurobiology at the University of Utah, told The Verge that “there are certainly some aspirations in this agenda that most US scientists would agree with: we need more stability, faster peer review, and more incentives to do high risk science.” But Shepherd said the document looks like it “was written by political appointees without any real consultation with scientists” and warned that its assumptions science functions like a business were misplaced. “Academic science is different to VC funded startups or tech companies.” It’s an important distinction to make considering Kratsios’ background. Unlike most White House science advisers, Kratsios is not a scientist in any sense of the word, and has no scientific credentials. He has a background in tech policy and finance, spending part of his working life at a fund run by Silicon Valley investor Peter Thiel. Researchers say the report is permeated by this Silicon Valley mindset, as well as a profound lack of scientific understanding. “The report has no vision for how science works,” said Harvard professor Jeffrey Flier, former dean of the university’s medical school, adding that it “seems blissfully unaware” of the academic environment scientific research needs in order to flourish. “This is completely insane as an approach to reforming US science funding and operations,” he said, branding the report’s proposals a “major threat” and an effort to politicize and control science. Other researchers I spoke to feel similarly. The government’s entire approach seems to be built on the “misguided belief that scientific breakthroughs in the future will come from the tech sector,” Andreas Karch, a physics professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told The Verge. “While American tech is also leading in their field, tech and science aren’t the same,” he said, adding that today’s scientific leadership will secure tomorrow’s tech leadership. “There is little evidence that our big tech companies, despite their stunning successes, can do both.” Not that the proposals make that much sense, either. “The agenda is rife with contradictions,” Shepherd said, pointing to a proposal that suggests radically reducing government support for “life sciences,” while increasing support for “foundational research in the biological sciences,” two categories that have substantial overlap. Neither the report nor the White House defines those terms or explains which fields would gain or lose funding. The narrow focus on AI is also “misguided,” Karch said. While there’s certainly a chance it will accelerate progress, he said “right now the problem is that most science done by AI is absolute slop.” Supervision by humans seems “absolutely key,” he said, but those humans are primarily trained by the universities having their funding slashed. “We may well end up in the situation where AI will have a few major insights buried under mountains of slop, and the number of people with the experience and knowledge to tell the two apart may rapidly dwindle,” he said, adding that the government’s actions are actually hindering scientists’ abilities to make use of these powerful new technologies. The funding and document arrive amid sweeping cuts, grant cancellations, and institutional upheaval across the entire federal funding system, rocking universities, research centers, and government agencies nationwide. Researchers say that reality is difficult to reconcile with the administration’s promise of a new “golden age” for American science. “As an outsider to the US system, this seems to be a further attempt at dismantling the US research universities,” said de Vreese. He called Kratsios’ vision “a fundamental departure from a very successful US science model” that looks like another attempt to “upend the US research university model.” That departure could spell disaster. Carl Bergstrom, a professor of biology at the University of Washington, told The Verge the plan fundamentally misunderstands and misrepresents the role US funding agencies play in the scientific endeavor. While they do in part promote technological discoveries and medical breakthroughs — key priorities in the report — they are also designed to “develop and perpetuate a vibrant STEM ecosystem in the US,” Bergstrom said. “This plan undercuts much of that role, and will have disastrous effects that will ricochet throughout the US economy in years to come.” That narrow view of science, focused on outcomes, applications, and measurable returns, is precisely what this new model gets wrong. It treats science like a business, which makes sense given Trump has said he runs the country like one. Most researchers who spoke to The Verge were deeply skeptical this plan would usher in the promised golden age of American science, with many warning it could cause lasting damage. For other groups, notably those closest to power, the future could look brighter. “This looks like a golden age for specific groups and likely for tech and venture capitalists,” de Vreese said. Shepherd said “academic science cannot be replaced by a business model.” Most research scientists seem to agree with that sentiment, but the Trump administration seems determined to try anyway.

articles.title: Cheetahs disappeared from Zambia's Greater Luangwa for nearly 30 years; six are back as conservationists rebuild the ecosystem
articles.summary: Six cheetahs have returned to Zambia’s Greater Luangwa Ecosystem after nearly three decades without confirmed sightings.
articles.body: Six cheetahs have returned to Zambia’s Greater Luangwa Ecosystem after nearly three decades without confirmed sightings. The 3 males and 3 females were moved from South Africa to a remote part of North Luangwa National Park in July 2026, beginning a carefully planned effort to rebuild a wild population. The project is not simply about releasing 6 animals. Conservationists have spent years assessing habitat, strengthening protection and working with communities so the wider landscape can support cheetahs again. The first arrivals are now being closely watched as the restoration effort moves into its most important stage.Cheetahs are returning to the Greater Luangwa EcosystemCheetahs were once part of the Luangwa Valley, but they disappeared from the region during the 1990s. The Cheetah Conservation Initiative says the last sighting was recorded in 1997. The disappearance is associated with successive anthrax outbreaks and wider human disturbance.The landscape has changed since then. According to Mongabay, conservation work in North Luangwa and South Luangwa national parks has helped produce healthier prey populations and allowed other large carnivores, including lions and African wild dogs, to flourish. However, cheetahs are unlikely to return naturally because the nearest viable populations are too far away and disconnected. That makes a planned reintroduction the practical route back.The Cheetah Conservation Initiative says planning began during the 2017–18 revision of Zambia’s National Conservation Action Plan, with the Luangwa Valley identified as suitable for cheetah recovery. The government formally approved the project in May 2024 after years of preparation and discussions with conservation partners and local communities.What makes North Luangwa suitable for the catsNorth Luangwa was selected after a detailed assessment rather than simply because cheetahs historically lived there. Africa Geographic reports that the Zoological Society of London used information on cheetah movements and habitat use from other locations to assess suitable areas in the Luangwa Valley. Four potential sites were compared before a remote southern section of North Luangwa National Park was chosen.The area also offers a mixture of habitats. Riverine woodland, floodplains, thickets and more open ground give cheetahs different places to hunt and move through. This variety could also help them avoid lions, leopards and spotted hyenas, all of which can compete with or kill cheetahs.Discover Africa notes that North Luangwa covers more than 4,500 square kilometres and contains riverine forests, open grasslands and prey such as impala and puku. The wider Greater Luangwa Ecosystem covers about 70,000 square kilometres, giving a wide-ranging species room to move beyond the initial release area.Preparing the six cheetahs for release into the wildThe first group consists of three males and three females selected from South Africa’s managed cheetah population. Wildlife Vagabond reports that the males include two brothers and a solitary male, while the females include two sisters and a solitary female. The animals underwent veterinary checks before being transported to Zambia.The selection was also based on qualities that could improve their chances of coping with North Luangwa. Africa Geographic reports that the founders were chosen for factors including age, sex, genetic diversity and previous experience living alongside competing predators. They came from South African reserves where they had already lived independently with lions and similar prey.The Cheetah Conservation Initiative describes a three-stage process. Preparing the landscape and communities, relocating and acclimatising the animals, and then releasing and monitoring them. The project built 4 holding bomas and a 2,000-hectare predator-proof sanctuary for the process.What happens before the cheetahs roam freelyThe cats are not being released straight into the wilderness. Discover Africa reports that they underwent quarantine before being flown to a remote part of southern North Luangwa, where they entered a two-stage soft-release process. The sanctuary allows them to become familiar with the surroundings before they move into the unfenced landscape.The Cheetah Conservation Initiative says the sanctuary is intended to encourage familiarity with the release area and support natural social behaviour and territory formation. The animals are also fitted with satellite and VHF tracking collars.8 trained Zambian monitors will follow the cheetahs, while veterinary and conservation teams will watch their health, movements, hunting behaviour and interactions with other animals. The information will help managers change future releases if the first animals face unexpected difficulties.Can six animals establish a lasting populationThe first 6 are only the beginning. Mongabay reports that another six cheetahs were moved in August 2026, with a third group of six planned for August 2027.Africa Geographic stresses that success will depend on whether the animals establish territories, breed and eventually survive with less need for additional animals from South Africa. Some could also disperse beyond North Luangwa towards other parts of the Greater Luangwa Ecosystem, including South Luangwa. Collar data will show whether the existing connections between protected areas are sufficient for those movements.Local communities remain part of the recoveryThe restoration effort also extends beyond wildlife management. The Cheetah Conservation Initiative says village consultations, land-use planning, school outreach, conservation agriculture training and local employment are part of the programme. Its community measures include Village Action Groups, chilli patrols and livestock recovery efforts designed to reduce problems between people and wildlife.Africa Geographic reports that the project provided 183 jobs in 2025 in the surrounding Munyamadzi Game Management Area, where formal employment opportunities are limited. The wider aim is to make conservation useful to people living around the landscape as well as to the animals being restored.

articles.title: In 1987, ancient glass sponge reefs were found alive off Canada's Pacific coast in B.C.'s Hecate Strait after being thought extinct for 40 million years; they survive today in three sounds
articles.summary: Far beneath the cold waters off British Columbia, an extraordinary ecosystem is thriving in near-total darkness, a vast network of reefs made not from
articles.body: Far beneath the cold waters off British Columbia, an extraordinary ecosystem is thriving in near-total darkness, a vast network of reefs made not from tropical coral, but from animals whose skeletons are built from silica, the same material found in glass.These are glass sponge reefs, and for decades scientists believed reef-building sponges of this kind had disappeared from Earth roughly 40 million years ago.Then, in 1987, Canadian scientists discovered that they were still alive.According to Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO), four major glass sponge reefs were discovered that year in Hecate Strait and were found to be more than 9,000 years old. The discovery revealed that an ecosystem once thought extinct had survived in the deep waters off Canada's Pacific coast.Today, these extraordinary formations are often described as the “Sea of Glass.”Reefs built by animals, not coralGlass sponges are marine animals whose intricate skeletons are made from silica. Unlike the soft-bodied sponges familiar from shallow waters, these deep-sea animals create rigid, glass-like structures.Some species are capable of building reefs. New generations of sponges settle on the skeletons left behind by previous generations, gradually creating enormous mounds and ridges on the seafloor.DFO says the reefs can grow to hundreds of square kilometres and reach heights of up to 25 metres. The largest reefs in Hecate Strait and Queen Charlotte Sound lie between about 140 and 240 metres below the surface.The four major Hecate Strait reefs cover an area of about 1,000 square kilometres and are considered the largest living examples of glass sponge reefs that were once widespread during the Jurassic period.A prehistoric ecosystem that survivedThe story of these reefs goes back hundreds of millions of years.Glass sponge reefs were once common around the world, particularly during the Jurassic period. Fossil evidence shows that they formed extensive reef systems long before modern coral reefs dominated many marine environments.Scientists believed living reef-building glass sponges had disappeared approximately 40 million years ago.That assumption was overturned when Canadian scientists mapped the seafloor off British Columbia in the 1980s.Natural Resources Canada scientist Kim Conway, who was involved in the expeditions, recalled that researchers initially encountered unusual mounds and ridges without immediately understanding what they were. It took several expeditions and years of investigation before scientists determined that the formations were reefs created by sponges.The discovery was formally confirmed in 1987.Why these reefs exist off British ColumbiaGlass sponges can be found in oceans around the world, but the enormous reef formations are exceptionally rare.According to DFO, British Columbia's glass sponge reefs occur in Hecate Strait, Queen Charlotte Sound, the Strait of Georgia and Howe Sound. Most are found at depths between about 90 and 300 metres, although some reefs in Howe Sound occur much closer to the surface.The reefs require a particular combination of environmental conditions, including cold, nutrient-rich water and sufficient dissolved silica for the sponges to build their skeletons.These conditions have allowed the animals to survive and build reef structures over thousands of years.A giant filtration system beneath the PacificThe reefs are not simply remnants of prehistoric life. They are functioning ecosystems that continue to play an important role in the modern ocean.Glass sponges pump seawater through their bodies and filter microscopic organisms and particles from the water.Their enormous reef structures also provide shelter, refuge and nursery grounds for marine species, including rockfish, finfish and shellfish. DFO describes the reefs as important habitat for numerous aquatic species.The intricate structures effectively transform sections of the deep seafloor into complex underwater habitats, creating an oasis of marine life in otherwise relatively flat areas of the Pacific.Thousands of years to build, but easily damagedThe extraordinary age of these reefs also makes them extremely vulnerable.Their skeletons are made of silica and can be broken by physical contact. DFO warns that fishing gear and other activities that disturb the seafloor can damage the structures, while increased sediment can smother the sponges and interfere with their ability to survive.Recovery is exceptionally slow.DFO notes that individual glass sponges can live for more than 200 years, while recovery from significant reef damage could take tens to several hundreds of years. If the skeletons of dead sponges are destroyed or buried, new generations cannot use them as the foundation for further reef growth.Climate change is adding another concern, with scientists investigating how warming and changing ocean chemistry could affect the fragile organisms and the ecosystems they support.Canada created a marine protected areaThe discovery eventually led to major conservation measures.In 2017, Fisheries and Oceans Canada designated the Hecate Strait and Queen Charlotte Sound Glass Sponge Reefs as a Marine Protected Area.The protected area covers approximately 2,410 square kilometres and was created to conserve the biological diversity, structural habitat and ecosystem functions associated with the ancient reefs.The reefs are also on Canada's Tentative List for potential UNESCO World Heritage recognition because of their geological, biological and paleontological importance. Parks Canada describes them as a unique window into prehistoric marine ecosystems.One place where divers can see themMost of British Columbia's glass sponge reefs remain far too deep for recreational divers.But Howe Sound offers a remarkable exception.According to DFO, glass sponge reefs in Howe Sound can occur at depths of just 22 metres.At Halkett Point near Gambier Island, the reef lies in approximately 30 metres of water, making it one of the few places in the world where glass sponge reefs are accessible to both scientists and scuba divers. BC Parks says the marine area was specifically expanded in 2016 to protect the rare reef.For non-divers, conservation organisations have created educational resources and digital maps that allow people to explore the “Sea of Glass” without descending into the deep.A prehistoric world still aliveThe glass sponge reefs of British Columbia are remarkable precisely because they are not fossils.They are living ecosystems, descendants of a reef-building lineage that flourished when dinosaurs roamed the planet.For millions of years, scientists believed these reefs had disappeared. Their discovery in 1987 proved otherwise, revealing a hidden world that had continued growing in the darkness of the Pacific.Today, the “Sea of Glass” is both a scientific wonder and a conservation priority, an ancient ecosystem that survived for thousands of years, yet remains vulnerable to damage in a rapidly changing ocean.

articles.title: Meet Shrikari Punjala, the 7th grader who turned eggshells into calcium carbonate crystals that reduced bacterial growth
articles.summary: A seventh grader from Palatine, Illinois, has turned eggshells into calcium carbonate crystals and used them to investigate whether the mineral can affect
articles.body: A seventh grader from Palatine, Illinois, has turned eggshells into calcium carbonate crystals and used them to investigate whether the mineral can affect bacterial growth. Shrikari Punjala, a student at Quest Academy, is one of 30 finalists in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. Her project, “How Do Calcium Carbonate Crystals Affect Bacterial Growth?”, was inspired by her research into Sporosarcina pasteurii, a bacterium known for its role in calcium carbonate biomineralisation. She extracted calcium carbonate from eggshells using acetic acid, then tested the crystals against four bacterial species grown on agar plates. Society for Science reports that bacterial coverage after the crystals were added was 55% for Aeromonas sobria, 65% for Sporosarcina ureae, 66.25% for Escherichia coli and 71.25% for Bacillus subtilis. The organisation says the results showed that the calcium carbonate inhibited bacterial growth. As Finals Week approaches, Punjala's eggshell-derived research offers an intriguing early look at how a simple kitchen waste material might one day inform new approaches to controlling bacterial growth.Punjala joins the 2026 Junior Innovators Challenge top 30The Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge is run by Society for Science and is described by the organisation as the nation's premier STEM research competition for middle-school students. The 30 finalists were selected from the Top 300 Junior Innovators, who were chosen from 1,997 entrants. The finalists represent 17 states and Puerto Rico, with Environmental and Earth Sciences the most prevalent project category among them, according to Society for Science's 2026 finalist announcement and competition press release.The competition reaches about 60,000 students annually through Society for Science's Affiliated Fair network. Students qualify to enter by placing in the top 10% of participants at a Society-affiliated science fair. Every finalist receives a $500 cash award, while their schools receive $1,000 for STEM activities. During Finals Week in Washington, DC, from October 23 to 28, judges will assess the students' research and, in team challenges, their communication, creativity and collaboration. The finalist announcement also says critical thinking will be part of the evaluation. Away from her research, Punjala is active in tennis, badminton, pickleball and volleyball and is interested in debate. She says debate has strengthened her speaking skills and encouraged her to consider viewpoints different from her own. She has also participated in the Invention Convention, an experience she says sparked her interest in biomedical engineering. She describes biomedical engineering as a field that combines biology and invention.Why Punjala tested calcium carbonate against bacteriaPunjala's project began with Sporosarcina pasteurii, a soil bacterium that has been widely studied for its ability to contribute to calcium carbonate formation. A 2021 review published in Microorganisms describes S. pasteurii as a Gram-positive soil bacterium with very high urease activity and identifies it as the most frequently used strain in biomineralisation research. That research led Punjala to a different question: what happens when calcium carbonate is introduced to bacteria rather than being produced through bacterial activity? Society for Science reports that her reading suggested calcium carbonate might inhibit some bacterial species while allowing others to prosper, prompting her to test the mineral against several types of bacteria.For her source of calcium carbonate, Punjala used eggshells. A 2022 review in Frontiers in Materials reports that chicken eggshells contain about 94% to 97% calcium carbonate, predominantly in the calcite form. The review also examines methods for producing calcium carbonate from eggshells. Eggshell waste has also been studied as a material for other applications. A 2021 review in Sustainable Materials and Technologies titled “Food waste eggshell valorisation through development of new composites: A review” examines research into using eggshell waste in the development of composite materials and discusses its potential for waste valorisation.How the calcium carbonate experiment was conductedPunjala's experiment involved four bacterial species: Bacillus subtilis, Escherichia coli, Aeromonas sobria and Sporosarcina ureae. After obtaining calcium carbonate from eggshells with acetic acid, she grew the bacteria on agar plates and incubated them at 30°C for three days. She then added the calcium carbonate crystals and recorded the bacterial coverage, according to the Society for Science. Testing several species allowed Punjala to compare their responses to the same mineral. Her background research had suggested that calcium carbonate could affect different bacteria in different ways, giving her four species to examine in the experiment.Calcium carbonate reduced bacterial coverage in all four speciesSociety for Science reports that bacterial coverage after calcium carbonate was added was 55% for A. sobria, 65% for S. ureae, 66.25% for E. coli and 71.25% for B. subtilis. All four species showed lower reported coverage after the calcium carbonate was added. Society for Science concludes from the experiment that the calcium carbonate inhibited bacterial growth. The profile doesn't give starting coverage or plate counts. The experiment examined bacterial growth under the conditions used in Punjala's test. Its findings do not establish how calcium carbonate would affect other bacterial species or whether the same response would occur under different experimental conditions.Calcium carbonate and bacterial biomineralisationResearch into S. pasteurii has explored calcium carbonate biomineralisation for applications beyond the question tested by Punjala. The 2021 Microorganisms review discusses uses including self-healing concrete, bio-bricks, desert sand solidification and the disposal of harmful metals. Those applications involve using bacterial activity to produce or deposit calcium carbonate, whereas Punjala's experiment starts with calcium carbonate extracted from eggshells and examines its relationship with bacterial growth. The two areas therefore approach the mineral from different directions. Punjala's experiment adds eggshell-derived calcium carbonate to cultures of four bacterial species and measures the resulting bacterial coverage. The reported results showed lower coverage across all four species, with the largest reported reduction in the experiment occurring for A. sobria, at 55% coverage.From a school experiment to the national stagePunjala is now among the 30 students who will take their projects to the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge Finals Week in Washington, DC, from October 23 to 28. She will present her research alongside finalists from across the United States and Puerto Rico, bringing an experiment that began with eggshell-derived calcium carbonate into a national middle-school science competition.

articles.title: 3,000-year-old horse buried inside ancient Egyptian fortress may have been a chariot animal; rare discovery, Ramesses II and Libyan prisoner tablets also found
articles.summary: Archaeologists in Egypt have uncovered the carefully buried remains of a horse dating back around 3,000 years inside an ancient military fortress in the
articles.body: Archaeologists in Egypt have uncovered the carefully buried remains of a horse dating back around 3,000 years inside an ancient military fortress in the western Nile Delta, a rare discovery that is offering new clues about the role and cultural importance of horses in ancient Egyptian warfare.The horse was discovered at the archaeological site of Abqaa’, in Egypt’s Lake District. The fortress dates to the New Kingdom period, around 1550 to 1070 B.C., and was built to protect Egypt’s western frontier from hostile Libyan groups.According to Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, the horse was a young, medium-sized male. Archaeologists also discovered pieces of its harness near the remains, suggesting that it may have been used to pull a chariot or participated in other military activities.Horse burial may have been ceremonialThe circumstances of the discovery indicate that the horse was deliberately buried rather than simply abandoned at the site. Egyptian authorities said the burial was likely ceremonial, suggesting the animal may have held considerable value.Experts unaffiliated with the excavation told Live Science that the discovery is particularly significant because complete horse remains from Pharaonic Egypt are uncommon.Lonneke Delpeut, a researcher at the University of Vienna who has studied ancient Egyptian horses, described the find to Live Science as an “amazing find.” She noted that archaeologists know of ancient Egyptian horse stables, including those at Pi-Ramesses, but actual horse remains are much harder to find.Delpeut cautioned against definitively labeling the animal a “war horse,” explaining that there is no clear definition of the term in the context of ancient Egypt. However, she said the evidence indicates that it was certainly a chariot horse.Horses transformed transportation and warfare in ancient Egypt, making an animal associated with a military fortress potentially particularly valuable.Fortress was built to guard Egypt’s western frontierThe discovery provides insight into the strategic importance of Abqaa’. The fortress was established during the New Kingdom, when Egypt maintained a series of defensive installations along its western frontier.The region faced threats from various Libyan groups, including the Meshwesh, with whom ancient Egypt frequently came into conflict.Archaeologists found a tablet depicting a Libyan prisoner. According to the Egyptian ministry, the man’s clothing identifies him as a member of the Meshwesh tribe.The prisoner is shown with his hands tied behind his back and his body bent forward, a posture that represented submission.Ramesses II and Merneptah inscriptions discoveredThe excavation also uncovered inscriptions associated with two major New Kingdom pharaohs.One hieroglyphic tablet bears the name of Ramesses II, who ruled Egypt from approximately 1279 to 1213 B.C.A second tablet mentions Merneptah, who ruled from approximately 1213 to 1203 B.C. The inscription compares Merneptah’s strength to that of Seth, the ancient Egyptian god associated with the desert and storms.Together, the discoveries provide evidence of the fortress’s role during a period when Egypt was defending its borders while projecting military power beyond them.Experts say horse could reveal more about ancient warfareCarolyn Willekes, an expert on ancient horses at Mount Royal University in Canada, told Live Science that well-preserved horse remains can provide valuable information about the life of an individual animal.The apparent intentional burial is particularly intriguing because it could reveal more about how ancient Egyptians viewed and valued horses.The nearby harness fittings could also help researchers understand the animal’s use, while scientific analysis of the skeleton may potentially provide additional information about its age, health and working life.The excavation was carried out by an archaeological team from Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.For researchers, the discovery is significant not only because of the horse’s age but because it combines rare skeletal remains, military equipment and a carefully arranged burial inside a fortress built on one of ancient Egypt’s contested frontiers.

articles.title: Gabe Newell has put more than $816 million into deep-sea research; his Inkfish fleet is building a 162-metre science vessel
articles.summary: Gabe Newell’s marine research organisation Inkfish has ordered a 162-metre deep-sea research vessel from Norwegian shipbuilder VARD.
articles.body: Gabe Newell’s marine research organisation Inkfish has ordered a 162-metre deep-sea research vessel from Norwegian shipbuilder VARD. The ship, named RV11000, is valued at nearly €700 million, or about $816 million, and is scheduled for delivery in the first quarter of 2030. According to Marine Insight, the vessel will be designed to work at depths of up to 11,000 metres, allowing it to support some of the deepest ocean research missions. The project is VARD’s largest order ever for a single vessel and will expand Inkfish’s ability to study remote parts of the ocean.Capabilities of Gabe Newell’s 162-metre deep-sea vesselRV11000 is being developed specifically for deep-ocean scientific work rather than general-purpose shipping. Fincantieri, VARD’s parent group, said the vessel will be used for seafloor mapping, coring and sampling, submarine operations and remotely operated vehicle missions.The ship will be 162 metres long and 28 metres wide. Its design is based on the VARD 9 42 platform and has been developed by Vard Design in Alesund, Norway, with Inkfish and technical partner YTMC. Fincantieri said the project builds on the engineering and design foundations of RV6000, a 100-metre research vessel that VARD began building for Inkfish after a contract signed in 2025.The scale of the new ship reflects the demands of reaching the deepest parts of the ocean. According to Marine Insight, RV11000 will be able to support underwater missions at depths of up to 11,000 metres, bringing the full depth of the ocean within the vessel’s planned operating range.How will RV11000 handle demanding underwater missionsThe vessel will carry equipment for launching, recovering and supporting several types of underwater vehicles. Marine Insight reports that this will include a stern-mounted A-frame, systems for remotely operated vehicles, shipboard cranes and an offshore crane.There will also be a dedicated hangar for two submarines and another area for ROV operations. The ship will have a coring system, scientific winches, a moonpool, hatches and a drop keel to support different forms of ocean research.Fincantieri said the hull has been optimised for seafloor mapping, while advanced stabilisers are intended to reduce movement during scientific operations. The vessel will also use a propulsion system combining direct-current technology with battery power.Importance of the large battery for scientific workOne of RV11000’s most notable features is its battery installation. VARD says the ship will have one of the largest battery systems ever fitted to a vessel, with enough capacity to allow up to 12 hours of silent scientific operations.That capability is particularly relevant when researchers need to reduce noise and vibration around underwater equipment. Rather than relying entirely on conventional propulsion during every stage of a mission, the vessel will be able to use its battery system for periods when quieter operation is important.Marine Insight also reports that the battery system will work with the vessel’s propulsion arrangement to improve flexibility and efficiency. The ship will additionally be built to meet the latest cybersecurity requirements set by the International Association of Classification Societies.New underwater technology available on the vesselKongsberg Maritime is supplying a specialised system that will change how autonomous underwater vehicles are handled aboard the ship. In its September 2026 announcement, Kongsberg said it had secured a contract to provide an autonomous underwater vehicle hangar and launch and recovery system for the VARD-built Inkfish vessel.The system will allow HUGIN autonomous underwater vehicles to be launched, recovered and docked below the sea surface. Kongsberg said moving these operations beneath the wave zone can reduce the effect of waves, improving safety and allowing missions to continue in higher sea states.The delivery will include the hangar integration, a skidding system, vehicle logistics and an overhead crane for handling the underwater vehicles. Kongsberg said the equipment is expected to be assembled and tested in Norway, with delivery planned for the end of 2027.How will scientists use the ship during long expeditionsRV11000 is being designed to accommodate the people and facilities needed for extended research missions. Fincantieri said the vessel will provide accommodation for up to 130 crew members and researchers, alongside laboratories, workshops and dedicated scientific spaces.Marine Insight also reports that the ship will have laboratories, offices, workshops and public areas intended to support long-duration missions. Most of the people aboard will be housed in single cabins, giving the vessel the capacity to function as a large research base while operating far from shore.Inkfish also intends for the research carried out through its vessels to contribute data to open scientific repositories. This gives the ship a role beyond individual expeditions, as information gathered during missions can become part of a wider body of scientific knowledge.Location of construction for this 162-metre vesselThe construction process will involve VARD facilities in both Romania and Norway. Fincantieri said the hull of RV11000 will be built at Vard Shipyards Romania in Tulcea, while outfitting, commissioning and final delivery will take place at one of VARD’s shipyards in Norway.The project also marks another stage in Inkfish’s growing research fleet. Marine Insight notes that RV11000 will join RV Hydra and RV Dagon, while the earlier RV6000 is already under construction. Together, the vessels are intended to give Inkfish greater capacity to support marine research around the world.

articles.title: Trump entregará principal honraria científica dos EUA a Elon Musk e outros executivos da tecnologia | G1
articles.standfirst: Sergei Brin, cofundador do Google, e Jensen Huang, diretor-executivo da Nvidia, também estão entre os homenageados. Segundo a Casa Branca, a iniciativa é um agradecimento às 'contribuições desses líderes extraordinários em ciência e tecnologia'.
articles.summary: Sergei Brin, cofundador do Google, e Jensen Huang, diretor-executivo da Nvidia, também estão entre os homenageados. Segundo a Casa Branca, a iniciativa é um agradecimento às 'contribuições desses líderes extraordinários em ciência e tecnologia'.
articles.body:
O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, e o fundador e CEO da SpaceX e da xAI, Elon Musk, falam com jornalistas na entrada da Casa Branca após um almoço com líderes do setor de tecnologia na Sala Leste, em Washington. — Foto: Jonathan Ernst / Reuters

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump , entregará nesta quinta-feira (8) a Elon Musk e a outros executivos da área de tecnologia a mais alta honraria científica do país, informou a Casa Branca .

O cofundador do Google, Sergei Brin, o diretor-executivo da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, e a diretora-geral da AMD, Lisa Su, também receberão a Medalha Nacional de Ciência durante o evento "Ciência: Uma Nova Era de Ouro".

O magnata do setor Michael Dell e o diretor-executivo da Microsoft, Satya Nadella, receberão a Medalha Nacional de Tecnologia e Inovação, a principal honraria do setor.

"A Administração Trump agradece as contribuições desses líderes extraordinários em ciência e tecnologia. Esses homenageados ajudam a garantir que os Estados Unidos continuem liderando o mundo em inovação", declarou nesta quarta-feira a porta-voz da Casa Branca, Liz Huston, em comunicado à AFP.

Musk voltou a se aproximar de Trump após o desentendimento entre os dois no ano passado, motivado pela passagem do bilionário da SpaceX e da Tesla pelo governo, onde foi encarregado de reduzir os gastos federais.

Musk e Huang participaram, no fim de setembro, do jantar de Estado oferecido por Trump em homenagem ao presidente chinês, Xi Jinping.

Ao lado de outros executivos do setor, eles também estiveram na Casa Branca na semana passada para reuniões em que as empresas se comprometeram a adotar mecanismos de autorregulação no desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial.

articles.title: Padre Antônio Maria visita tenda de apoio a romeiros na Dutra | G1
articles.standfirst: Pároco esteve em uma tenda na altura do Jardim Satélite, em São José dos Campos, na manhã desta quarta-feira (7).
articles.summary: O padre Antônio Maria visitou a tenda Bem-Te-Vi em São José dos Campos para incentivar voluntários e romeiros que seguem em peregrinação pela Rodovia Dutra.
articles.body:
Padre Antônio Maria visita tenda de apoio a peregrinos — Foto: Reprodução/TV Vanguarda

O padre Antônio Maria marcou presença em uma das tendas de apoio ao peregrino, na Rodovia Presidente Dutra, em São José dos Campos , na manhã desta quarta-feira (7).

O religioso aproveitou o período da manhã para ir à tenda Bem-Te-Vi, localizada na altura do bairro Jardim Satélite. Em entrevista à TV Vanguarda , ele contou que ir de encontro aos peregrinos é um combustível a mais.

“Para mim é como chegar a um posto de gasolina e me reabastecer para continuar minha caminhada, mesmo com andador porque tudo isso que a gente vivencia nesses lugares em que os peregrinos recebem o apoio, tudo isso fala muito ao meu coração”, declarou.

Segundo o pároco, mesmo com dificuldades na caminhada, ele sempre tenta ir à tenda apoiar os romeiros.

“Esse trabalho eu acho maravilhoso. Mesmo com um pouquinho de esforço, eu quero vir para parabenizar a quem trabalha e para dizer que: confiem porque Deus vai recompensar”, acrescentou.

A visita aconteceu em meio ao período de maior movimento de romeiros que seguem pela Rodovia Presidente Dutra em direção a Aparecida , onde fica o Santuário Nacional de Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

A programação da Novena e Festa da Padroeira ocorre de 3 a 12 de outubro, quando é celebrado o dia de Nossa Senhora Aparecida, Padroeira do Brasil.

Neste período, milhares de peregrinos percorrem a rodovia a pé para chegar à Basílica e participar das celebrações. Neste ano, a concessionária que administra a Dutra estima mais de 40 mil romeiros no trajeto entre os dias 7 e 12 de outubro.

articles.title: Brasil nunca ganhou um Nobel, mas já teve 28 indicados; veja quem são  | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento nos registros oficiais do prêmio, de 1901 a 1975, inclui nomes como Carlos Chagas, Cesar Lattes, Dom Hélder Câmara e Jorge Amado.
articles.summary: Levantamento nos registros oficiais do prêmio, de 1901 a 1975, inclui nomes como Carlos Chagas, Cesar Lattes, Dom Hélder Câmara e Jorge Amado.
articles.body:
Em 125 anos de história, Brasil nunca levou o Nobel — Foto: GETTY IMAGES/BBC

Está aberta a temporada do Nobel. O prêmio tem 125 anos de história e, ao longo desse tempo, ao menos 28 nomes brasileiros já estiveram na lista de indicados, apesar de o país nunca ter levado um para casa.

Nesta quarta-feira (7), a academia anuncia o Nobel de Química. A expectativa brasileira estava no prêmio de Física, anunciado nesta terça-feira (6).

O g1 analisou os registros de indicações publicados pela Fundação Nobel desde 1901. Foram 215 indicações ligadas ao Brasil, que contemplam 27 pessoas e uma instituição : o Instituto Histórico e Geográfico Brasileiro, indicado ao Nobel da Paz em 1924.

Nas ciências, os casos mais conhecidos são os de Carlos Chagas e Cesar Lattes. Chagas descreveu em 1909 a doença que leva seu nome, identificando o parasita, o inseto transmissor (o barbeiro) e o quadro clínico, um feito até hoje inédito na medicina.

Cesar Lattes ao lado do microscópio em 1949 — Foto: Arquivo Central/Siarq-Unicamp

Já Lattes ajudou a descobrir, em 1947, o méson pi, partícula que ajuda a explicar o que mantém o núcleo dos átomos unido. Mas o Nobel de Física de 1950 ficou só com o chefe da equipe, o britânico Cecil Powell. Na época, era comum o prêmio ir apenas para o líder da pesquisa.

A maior parte das indicações citando brasileiros foi para o Nobel da Paz: ao todo, 13 nomeações.

E você pode se perguntar: o que faz o país nunca ter levado um prêmio desses para casa? Para a presidente da Academia Brasileira de Ciências (ABC), Helena Nader, o que explica isso não é a qualidade da ciência feita no Brasil, muito pelo contrário. Segundo ela, o prêmio ainda olha pouco para o Sul Global e suas descobertas.

O Brasil já esteve, inclusive, nas citações que dão base às pesquisas premiadas. Ou seja, sem o que foi feito aqui, alguns dos feitos não seriam possíveis. Mas, ainda assim, ficou de fora da premiação, como ocorreu em 2025 com o físico Amir Caldeira.

Quem foram os nomes já indicados ao Nobel

Quem são os brasileiros já indicados ao Nobel?

A lista de indicados fica em sigilo por 50 anos. Por isso, os dados oficiais mais recentes são de 1975 , e não é possível saber, pelos registros, se outros brasileiros entraram na disputa depois disso.

As indicações podem ser feitas mais de uma vez, por mais de uma pessoa ou instituição. Considerando o número de vezes em que foram indicados, os brasileiros apareceram nos pedidos de consideração para Estocolmo mais de 200 vezes.

Nem todos os nomes da lista são de brasileiros natos, mas há casos de naturalizados ou que atuavam no paí. É o caso do físico americano David Bohm, que dava aulas na Universidade de São Paulo (USP), e do bioquímico francês René Wurmser, professor no Rio de Janeiro. Já o químico austríaco Fritz Feigl veio para o Brasil fugindo do nazismo, trabalhou no Rio e depois se naturalizou brasileiro.

Lista dos nomes já indicados ao Nobel — Foto: Arte/g1

E por que o Brasil nunca ganhou o Nobel?

Para a presidente da Academia Brasileira de Ciências (ABC), Helena Nader, a ausência de um laureado brasileiro diz pouco sobre a pesquisa feita no país . Para ela, o Brasil tem ciência de ponta e de referência, mas o comitê tem dificuldade de reconhecer pesquisas de impacto feitas fora do eixo Sul Global.

Segundo ela, quando se trata da América Latina, os comitês "não conseguem enxergar" a relevância das descobertas.

Nader lembra o caso de Carlos Chagas, autor de um feito até hoje inédito na medicina: descrever sozinho uma doença do início ao fim, do parasita ao inseto transmissor e ao quadro clínico.

Carlos Chagas e a bebê Rita, uma das pacientes atendidas por ele — Foto: Prefeitura de Lassance/Divulgação

Outro é o de Lattes, um dos físicos mais influentes do país, cujas descobertas ajudaram a moldar a física de partículas moderna. Na época, era comum que o Nobel premiasse apenas o líder da equipe. Assim, o prêmio de 1950 ficou com Cecil Powell, chefe do laboratório onde Lattes trabalhava.

O que pesa, segundo Helena, é a engrenagem que leva um nome até Estocolmo. Uma descoberta relevante é condição necessária, mas não suficiente. A candidatura precisa de patrocinadores, ou seja, cientistas, instituições e governos que articulem apoio a ela ao longo dos anos.

"O que pesa para receber um Nobel não é só a descoberta. Se fosse apenas isso, o Brasil já figuraria entre os laureados. O problema é que para ganhar um Nobel tem que ter lobby e o Sul Global está distante da maioria dos laureados para fazer essa pressão", explica , afirma.

Nader lembra que a potência da pesquisa nacional se prova quando o Nobel coloca nos agradecimentos e nas referências dos trabalhos premiados cientistas brasileiros deixados de fora do prêmio.

É o caso do físico Amir Caldeira. O nome dele aparece no documento científico que embasou o Nobel de Física de 2025 . A teoria que ele formulou há mais de 40 anos serviu de ponto de partida para os pesquisadores premiados, mas ele ficou de fora.

"Nós estamos lá, só não com o prêmio. Infelizmente, nossa ciência é central a todos eles, mas nós somos periféricos. Por isso, permanecemos de fora", diz Helena.

articles.title: SpaceX busca US$ 40 bilhões para comprar chips de IA da Nvidia | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa negocia com grandes gestoras em meio à disputa por chips avançados; Morgan Stanley estima que infraestrutura de IA precisará de US$ 1,5 trilhão até 2028.
articles.summary: Com apoio de grandes gestoras, a SpaceX busca US$ 40 bilhões para adquirir chips de IA da Nvidia e fortalecer sua infraestrutura de inteligência artificial.
articles.body:
A SpaceX está negociando com bancos e gestoras de investimentos para conseguir US$ 40 bilhões (R$ 200 bilhões) para comprar chips de inteligência artificial da Nvidia , segundo duas fontes ouvidas pela agência de notícias Reuters.

A empresa de Elon Musk também negocia com a PIMCO, uma das maiores gestoras de investimentos do mundo, para conseguir parte do dinheiro, afirmou uma das fontes.

De acordo com uma das fontes, a SpaceX pretende conseguir cerca de US$ 10 bilhões em empréstimos bancários e outros US$ 30 bilhões com a venda de títulos de dívida classificados como grau de investimento.

O dinheiro será usado para financiar a compra dos chips.

Uma transmissão ao vivo mostra o CEO da SpaceX, Elon Musk, no dia da oferta pública inicial (IPO) da SpaceX no Nasdaq MarketSite, na cidade de Nova York, EUA, 12 de junho de 2026. — Foto: REUTERS/Jeenah Moon

De acordo com o Financial Times, a gestora de investimentos Apollo deverá liderar o acordo com a SpaceX e ajudar a distribuir a dívida entre diferentes investidores.

SpaceX e Nvidia não comentaram sobre o assunto. Apollo e PIMCO se recusaram a comentar. As fontes ouvidas pelas Reuters pediram para não serem identificadas porque o acordo ainda não foi divulgado.

O financiamento mostra quanto dinheiro as empresas de tecnologia estão buscando para acompanhar o crescimento da inteligência artificial. Elas disputam chips mais avançados e investem na construção da infraestrutura necessária para desenvolver sistemas de IA.

O Morgan Stanley estima que a infraestrutura de IA precisará de US$ 1,5 trilhão em financiamento externo até 2028 . Ao mesmo tempo, credores e investidores estão cada vez mais cautelosos em financiar a expansão do setor .

As ações da SpaceX caíram 2% no início do pregão, enquanto as ações da Nvidia subiram 0,5%.

Musk, que abriu o capital da SpaceX em junho com uma oferta pública inicial (IPO) recorde de US$ 86 bilhões, afirmou no mês passado que o data center Colossus 2, da xAI, poderia mais que dobrar até dezembro o número de chips da Nvidia usados pela empresa .

Musk também disse que a xAI planeja usar exclusivamente equipamentos da Nvidia para construir seus data centers.

Em agosto, a Nvidia , principal fornecedora de processadores de IA, firmou parceria com Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs e KKR em plataformas de financiamento destinadas a mobilizar mais de US$ 500 bilhões para projetos de infraestrutura de IA.

articles.title: In 1872, a British planter released just 9 mongooses in Jamaica to kill rats; within a decade, they had spread across the island
articles.summary: In 1872, British planter William Bancroft Espeut released 9 small Indian mongooses into his sugar fields in Jamaica after importing them from India to
articles.body: In 1872, British planter William Bancroft Espeut released 9 small Indian mongooses into his sugar fields in Jamaica after importing them from India to control rats. Within 10 years, botanist Daniel Morris reported that the animals were abundant across the island and had reached elevations of 5,000 feet. The introduction later became associated with declines in Jamaican birds and reptiles, while the mongoose itself became the subject of a much broader debate about biological control and the unintended consequences of introducing animals. Historian Matthew Holmes of the University of Stavanger examined the episode in a 2023 study published in The British Journal for the History of Science titled A plague of weasels and ticks: animal introduction, ecological disaster, and the balance of nature in Jamaica, 1870–1900. Later ecological research has provided direct evidence of mongoose predation on threatened Jamaican species, while genetic research suggests that Jamaica experienced multiple mongoose introductions from India rather than a population descended solely from Espeut's original 9 animals. The mongoose's complicated legacy in Jamaica remains a cautionary case study in ecology, illustrating how even well-intentioned species introductions can trigger cascading, long-lasting effects that researchers are still working to fully understand.Why Espeut brought mongooses to JamaicaEspeut was a landholder and Fellow of the Linnaean Society who was struggling with rats on his Spring Garden Estate. His wife, Bessie Adela Jeannette Espeut, suggested using a mongoose after her own experience in Ceylon. In Espeut's account, she had previously owned an Indian mongoose as a pet and had seen it kill rats. He subsequently asked the Jamaican government to import mongooses from India. Holmes records that 4 males and 5 females arrived in February 1872, and Espeut immediately released them into his sugar fields. Espeut later reported that evidence of reduced rat damage was clear within 6 months. Holmes argues that Espeut's decision was based solely on his wife's experience with her pet, rather than on evidence about how a population of wild mongooses would behave after release. The date also has a historical discrepancy. Holmes uses February 1872 on the basis of Espeut's published account, while Espeut later gave American ornithologist William Earl Dodge Scott a different date, saying the animals had arrived in March 1873.The original 9 were not necessarily the only mongooses brought to Jamaica around this period. Holmes notes that several captive-bred mongooses were also sent from London around 1872, although those animals reportedly did not catch rats. Meanwhile, mongooses from Espeut's estate were trapped and sold to other Jamaican planters, helping the animals become established elsewhere on the island. Modern genetic research provides another reason not to treat the first 9 animals as the sole founders of Jamaica's mongoose population. A 2021 study in Biological Invasions titled “Dispersal history of a globally introduced carnivore, the small Indian mongoose Urva auropunctata, with an emphasis on the Caribbean region” analysed genetic data from 496 mongooses and found evidence consistent with multiple introductions into Jamaica from India. The molecular results also suggested that mongooses subsequently spread from Jamaica to Grenada and Puerto Rico, consistent with historical records.What the mongoose did after spreadingThe mongoose's expansion changed the original calculation behind its introduction. Reports from Jamaica increasingly described an animal that ate more than rats. In a USDA report published in 1899, Theodore Sherman Palmer, assistant chief of the Biological Survey, recorded mongooses preying on young livestock, poultry, ground-nesting birds, eggs, reptiles and other animals. The reports reflected growing concern that the predator was affecting species that had not been the target of the original rat-control effort. Modern research has supplied stronger evidence for some of those historical concerns. In a 2011 study published in Biological Invasions titled “Conservation implications of small Indian mongoose (Herpestes auropunctatus) predation in a hotspot within a hotspot: The Hellshire Hills, Jamaica,” Delano S. Lewis, Rick van Veen and Byron S. Wilson examined the stomach contents of 217 mongooses. They found that invertebrates and lizards accounted for 93% of identified prey items. The researchers also found remains of threatened species, including the blue-tailed galliwasp.Another study focused on the critically endangered Jamaican rock iguana. In a 2017 paper in The Herpetological Journal titled “Predation of Jamaican rock iguana (Cyclura collei) nests by the invasive small Asian mongoose (Herpestes auropunctatus) and the conservation value of predator control,” Rick van Veen and Byron S. Wilson monitored iguana nests and used motion-activated cameras to document mongoose predation. They found high nest-predation pressure attributable to mongooses and a significant reduction in predation within an experimental mongoose-removal area. The IUCN Iguana Specialist Group reports that mongooses depredated every monitored nest outside the control zone.Historical reports linked mongooses to disappearing birdsThe impact on Jamaica's birds was also documented by Outram Bangs and Frederick H. Kennard, who compiled a list of the island's birds in 1920. They reported that many species they had previously encountered were no longer present and attributed many of the changes to the mongoose. Among the birds they discussed was the “blue mountain duck,” which Holmes identifies as probably referring to Pterodroma caribbaea, a name associated with the Jamaican petrel. Bangs and Kennard reported that the bird had been driven to extinction by the mongoose. They also wrote that the common or helmeted guineafowl had apparently been exterminated in the wild by the predator. Holmes notes that the guineafowl was a naturalised bird introduced to Jamaica, rather than a native Jamaican species.The limpkin, meanwhile, had become restricted to 1 location by 1910, with Bangs and Kennard suggesting that the mongoose had found the species easy prey and contributed to its near extinction. Their account also recorded an example of a species that appeared to adapt. The whistling tree-duck, which had initially declined, was reported to have changed its breeding habits in some way, probably keeping its young in places too wet for the mongoose to hunt, after which it appeared to be regaining its former abundance.The disputed story about ticksThe mongoose was later drawn into another ecological explanation involving Jamaica's growing tick problem. As birds and reptiles declined, some observers argued that the loss of animals that fed on insects had allowed ticks and other pests to increase. By the 1890s, the idea had developed into a broader claim that nature was restoring its own balance by allowing ticks to attack the mongoose.Holmes finds little evidence for that explanation. Robert Newstead, who investigated Jamaica's tick problem in the early 20th century, found that mongooses appeared to be remarkably free from tick infestation. Holmes also notes that Jamaica's expanding cattle industry and imported livestock offered a more plausible explanation for the growth of the tick population. A later study by Gordon B. Thompson likewise found very few ticks on mongooses. The idea nevertheless became influential because it offered a neat explanation for an ecological disaster. If the mongoose had disrupted the island's wildlife and caused ticks to increase, then the supposed decline of the mongoose from tick infestations could be presented as nature correcting the disturbance. Holmes describes this as a post hoc rationalisation of the consequences of the introduction rather than an explanation established by evidence.

articles.title: Scientists breed one of America’s rarest rattlesnakes for the first time; six New Mexico ridge-nosed rattlesnake babies could help restore wild populations
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Zoo has announced the first litters born under Project Obscurus, an international recovery programme for the New Mexico ridge-nosed
articles.body: The Los Angeles Zoo has announced the first litters born under Project Obscurus, an international recovery programme for the New Mexico ridge-nosed rattlesnake. According to the Los Angeles Zoo's press release on 1 September 2026, a litter of five was born on 18 August and a single neonate on 28 August, making six neonates. The species is classified as Threatened by the US Fish and Wildlife Service and is widely considered the rarest rattlesnake in the United States. The zoo says the young snakes will be candidates for release in Arizona or New Mexico to bolster genetic diversity in struggling wild populations.How were six New Mexico ridge-nosed rattlesnake babies bornAccording to the LA Zoo, one litter of five neonates was born on 18 August, and a single neonate was born separately on 28 August. The zoo says these are the first-ever litters born as part of the breeding efforts for Project Obscurus. It is the first of the Project Obscurus partners to successfully breed this federally threatened species, and it expects other partners to follow.The release quotes Byron Wusstig, Curator of Ectotherms at the Los Angeles Zoo. According to Wusstig, the success reflects the animal care team's expertise in managing montane pit vipers. He says the two litters represent "a tangible lifeline" for a species whose numbers have drastically declined in the US. He also says that being the first partner to welcome litters shows the collaborative, science-based approach is working well.How does Project Obscurus help rattlesnake populationsProject Obscurus builds on more than three decades of continuous research and conservation work on the species in the United States and Mexico, beginning in the early 1990s. The zoo says that earlier work established much of the scientific foundation and field knowledge behind the current programme. Project Obscurus was formalised in 2024, with The Rattlesnake Conservancy coordinating the collaborative recovery efforts. The conservation-breeding partnership includes the Los Angeles Zoo, the Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum and the San Antonio Zoo, working alongside researchers, wildlife agencies and conservation partners in both countries.Project Obscurus is a collaborative headstart breeding programme designed to bolster and diversify the genetics of wild US populations. According to the zoo's "About Project Obscurus" section, the project involves researchers from the US and Mexico and cooperation with 10 natural resource agencies, as well as zoos, non-profits, independent researchers and volunteers. Its stated aims include better understanding environmental factors such as temperature and humidity, and continuing efforts to find more rattlesnakes near areas where they have previously been found. It also aims to set up head-starting at the three partner institutions, to carry out genetic rescue within the existing U.S. range, and to give the public more information about the snake.Why is it called a "sky island" snakeThe New Mexico ridge-nosed rattlesnake is widely considered the rarest rattlesnake in the United States and among the most imperilled in North America. The US Fish and Wildlife Service classifies it as Threatened. The release describes it as a small, pale grey to grey-brown pit viper known for its shy nature and characteristic upturned snout. It adds that, unlike many reptiles, the species is live-bearing, meaning it does not lay eggs.The subspecies is found in a small area of the US and Mexico. That area consists of the Peloncillo Mountains in Arizona and New Mexico, the Animas Mountains of New Mexico, and the Sierra San Luis of Sonora and Chihuahua. The release calls it a "sky island" snake, limited to montane habitats between 5,000 and 8,000 feet (approximately 1,500 to 2,500 metres) in elevation. There it relies primarily on humid woodlands and sometimes grassy slopes. Its high level of endemism, meaning it is restricted to a small, fragmented area, puts the subspecies at greater risk of catastrophic population decline.How could the snakes boost genetic diversityThe zoo staff will care for the six neonates behind the scenes. The zoo says that once they mature and reach appropriate benchmarks, the snakes and their offspring will become candidates for release into their native habitats in Arizona or New Mexico. There, the zoo says, they would directly support struggling wild populations by bolstering genetic diversity. The zoo credits the births to years of cross-border collaboration involving volunteers, researchers, the US Fish and Wildlife Service and numerous international partners in both countries.

articles.title: Nobel Prize in chemistry awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai
articles.summary: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of “non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.”
articles.body: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of “non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.” Kagan discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions, allowing a greater excess of one of the mirror images to be created than was previously assumed possible. His discovery has been revolutionary for chemists who develop reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, flavours, scents and new materials. Meanwhile, Soai designed the first chemical reaction in which only one of the potential mirror images was formed. Other than life itself, no one had ever achieved this feat. The Soai reaction is one of the most spectacular chemical experiments ever conducted, the Nobel Committee for Chemistry said. “Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously,” Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. “The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular.” Kagan, 95, born in France, is affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and Soai, born in Japan, with the Tokyo University of Science. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm. Last year, three scientists won the chemistry Nobel for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside, laying the groundwork to potentially suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere or harvest moisture from desert environments. This year’s prizes began with the Nobel for medicine, awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award Tuesday recognized a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The literature prize is set to be awarded Thursday. After Friday’s peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.
