articles.title: Prince William’s Earthshot Prize says its Finalists have protected or restored 58 million hectares of land and improved 85 million hectares of ocean and coastline since 2020
articles.summary: The Earthshot Prize, the environmental award launched by Prince William, says its community of 75 Finalists supported since 2020 has protected or restored
articles.body: The Earthshot Prize, the environmental award launched by Prince William, says its community of 75 Finalists supported since 2020 has protected or restored 58 million hectares of land, forests and freshwater systems and protected, restored or improved 85 million hectares of ocean and coastline. The figures come from the Prize's 2025/26 Impact Report and were repeated when it announced its 15 Finalists for 2026 in September. The Prize also says its Finalists have avoided or captured more than 18 million tonnes of CO₂e emissions, removed or avoided 465,000 tonnes of waste, saved 21 million tonnes of water and improved air quality in regions home to 600 million people. The figures are reported by the Earthshot Prize and are not presented as independently audited totals. The 2026 Finalists will compete for 5 £1 million prizes at the Earthshot Prize Awards Night in Mumbai on 17 November.Earthshot Prize impact: 58 million hectares of land and 85 million hectares of oceanThe Prize's impact page says that, since being selected, its Finalists have protected, restored or improved 85 million hectares of ocean and coastline and protected and restored 58 million hectares of land, forests and freshwater systems. It also reports 18 million tonnes of CO₂e emissions avoided or captured and 465,000 tonnes of waste removed, upcycled or avoided. The Prize's June 2026 impact update additionally reported 21 million tonnes of water saved, reused or recycled and improved air quality in regions home to 600 million people. The figures describe different forms of environmental work and should not be interpreted as 143 million unique hectares. The 2 categories also use different definitions: the land figure covers land, forests and freshwater systems that have been protected and restored, while the ocean figure includes ocean and coastline that have been protected, restored and improved. The Prize does not state whether the areas in the 2 figures are mutually exclusive.The impact page gives examples of the work behind these figures. The Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative now protects more than 5 million hectares of Kazakhstan's steppe and supports the recovery and reintroduction of native endangered species including Przewalski's horses. The Prize also highlights the Great Bubble Barrier, which it says has captured more than one million pieces of plastic in Amsterdam since its installation, and Equatic, which it says has secured $11.6 million in new funding to support a carbon dioxide removal facility in Singapore. These are figures and descriptions reported by the Earthshot Prize on its impact platform. The Prize also reports financial activity associated with its wider Finalist network. It says the Tropical Forest Forever Facility and Bonds for Ocean Conservation have secured $6.8 billion in new finance commitments, while early-stage for-profit Finalists have raised $500 million and non-profit and social enterprise Finalists have raised $300 million in funding and investment. The Prize separately says its digital content has been viewed 1.5 billion times since launch.Earthshot Prize 2026 Finalists: 15 solutions across 5 environmental categoriesThe 2026 cohort is the 6th group of Earthshot Finalists. The 15 solutions were selected from nearly 7,000 nominations across 169 countries, with support from more than 363 nominators and an Expert Advisory Panel of more than 150 specialists. The Finalists are competing across 5 categories: Revive Our Oceans, Fix Our Climate, Build a Waste-Free World, Protect and Restore Nature, and Clean Our Air. The cohort includes Satellites on Fire, an Argentinian AI-powered wildfire detection and alert platform operating across 21 countries; Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, which the Prize says now sells more electric three-wheelers than any other company in India; Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative, which is working to reconnect a mountain landscape across Canada and the United States; and the Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance, or ZEMBA, which brings cargo owners together to make commitments to zero-emission shipping. Other Finalists include Ørsted, AirQo, Pula and the Indigenous Desert Alliance.The 2026 selection process also introduced the science of positive tipping points across all 5 Earthshot selection criteria. The Prize says it worked with the University of Exeter and drew on the research of Professor Tim Lenton to develop a framework covering 51 solution areas across nature, air, oceans, waste and climate. It defines a positive tipping point as a point at which beneficial change becomes self-reinforcing, allowing progress to accelerate with less external support. The scientific concept is discussed in a review article published in Global Sustainability titled Operationalising positive tipping points towards global sustainability. Published online on 10 January 2022, the paper by Tim Lenton and colleagues examines how relatively small interventions can trigger self-reinforcing feedbacks that accelerate change toward sustainability. The authors discuss positive tipping points across social, technological and ecological systems and outline ways such points might be identified and deliberately encouraged.Earthshot Prize Awards 2026 in Mumbai: how the impact figures compare with the 30x30 targetThe 2026 winners will be announced at the Earthshot Prize Awards Night in Mumbai on 17 November. The event is sponsored by the Serum Institute of India and will be hosted by Indian filmmaker and broadcaster Karan Johar. Each of the 5 Winners will receive £1 million to scale their work, while all 15 Finalists will receive mentorship, resources and technical support through the Prize's network. The Earthshot figures provide one measure of the environmental activity attributed by the Prize to its Finalist community, but they cannot be directly converted into progress toward the global 30x30 conservation target. Under Target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, countries committed to effectively conserving at least 30% of terrestrial and inland water areas and 30% of marine and coastal areas by 2030.The latest Protected Planet statistics, updated in October 2026, show that protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures cover 18.69% of terrestrial and inland waters and 10.04% of marine areas. That leaves roughly 11.3 percentage points of terrestrial and inland-water coverage and 20 percentage points of marine coverage to reach 30%. Those remaining figures are simple calculations from the current coverage statistics, rather than figures published by Protected Planet. The situation at sea has changed significantly in 2026. The International Union for Conservation of Nature said in April 2026 that 10.01% of the world's ocean was within protected and conserved areas, calling the figure an important global milestone and noting that the former Aichi target of 10% by 2020 had been reached six years late. IUCN also stressed that coverage alone is not enough: protected and conserved areas need effective management and equitable governance to deliver conservation outcomes.That distinction is important when interpreting the Earthshot Prize's 58 million and 85 million hectare figures. The Prize is reporting areas affected by the work of its Finalists, including areas protected, restored or improved. Protected Planet, by contrast, tracks formally documented protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures. The Earthshot Prize does not state how much of its reported land or ocean area overlaps with those internationally documented areas.

articles.title: Nobel Chemistry 2026: How Kagan, Soai solved century-old 'mirror-image' mystery
articles.summary: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 2026 has been awarded to France's Henri B Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai.
articles.body: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 2026 has been awarded to France's Henri B Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai. The scientists solved more than a century-old puzzle about why living organisms are made of one type of amino acids despite the existence of two similar mirror types in nature, and how a single type could be artificially produced so that the pharmaceuticals made from them do not exhibit harmful side effects on the human body.If we hold up our hands. they are mirror images of each other, yet no matter how you turn them, you cannot lay one perfectly over the other. Many molecules share this property. They come in two mirror-image forms, called left-handed and right-handed, built from the same atoms connected in the same order.Chemists call this property “chirality”, from the Greek word for hand, and such molecules are called “chiral” molecules.A world of one-handed moleculesHowever, life is strikingly one-sided.Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins making up our body, exist in both left- and right-handed forms, but the proteins in our cells are built almost exclusively from the left-handed kind. The right-handed versions are rare in nature. Chemists call this uniformity “homochirality”, or the “same hand".The puzzle is that ordinary chemistry, the one in our labs, has no such preference. When chemists ran reactions capable of producing these amino acids, they always got an equal 50/50 mixture. Nothing in the flask favoured one hand.Since we know the drugs that treat us are produced in labs, they were based on amino acids that existed in the 50/50 mixture. However, since the body is made of one-handed molecules, a drug's two mirror images can behave very differently. One may heal, while the other does nothing, or worse, have harmful side effects.Pharmaceutical chemists have long needed to make only the useful version.This phenomenon gives us two questions that were profoundly answered by Kagan and Soai’s contributions:How did life end up with just one? And how could chemists produce a single hand on purpose?Kagan: A surprising amplificationThe standard approach is to use a catalyst, a helper molecule that speeds up a reaction, which is itself single-handed and steers the reaction toward one hand. The common assumption was that a catalyst that is only partly pure should give a product that is also partly pure.In 1986, Henri Kagan found this was not always true. Sometimes an impure catalyst produced a much purer product than expected. The likely explanation is that left- and right-handed catalyst molecules pair up with one another and become locked into inactive duos, much like left and right gloves put away together in a drawer. The unpaired leftovers, all of one hand, do the real work.This "nonlinear effect" showed that a greater excess of one mirror image was achievable.Soai: a reaction that amplifies itselfKenso Soai took the idea further. In 1995, he published work describing a reaction with the potential to become fully homochiral, or “one-handed”.The trick was autocatalysis, in which the product of the reaction also acts as the catalyst for making more of itself.For example, by chance, a little more right-handed product forms at the start. That small excess catalyses the creation of still more right-handed product, which speeds things up further.Each cycle magnifies the imbalance, like a snowball rolling downhill.In 2003, Soai achieved the result, i.e a reaction that ended with only one of the two mirror images. Which hand wins in any given flask is a matter of chance, but each flask ends up single-handed. Before this, no one had matched what life itself does.Why it mattersFor medicine. Many drugs must be made as a single mirror image to be safe and effective. Kagan's and Soai's ideas gave chemists new strategies for designing such reactions, which also reduces waste, since half a batch is no longer discarded.Soai's reaction demonstrates that for the origin of life, an extremely small, random asymmetry can snowball into complete one-handedness without outside guidance.“Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular,” said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.

articles.title: Google invests millions in Mark Zuckerberg’s efforts to create a ‘virtual cell’
articles.summary: Google, Meta, and Isomorphic Labs are collectively investing $300 million into Biohub, the nonprofit biomedical research organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg.
articles.body: Google DeepMind, Meta, and AI drug discovery startup Isomorphic Labs are jointly investing $300 million into an initiative to create a “virtual cell” that researchers can use to combat disease, as reported earlier by Reuters. The project is led by Biohub, a nonprofit biomedical research organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan. It comes as part of a $1.8 billion “Virtual Biology” initiative to build AI datasets that could allow researchers to “ask, predict, and answer biological questions digitally.” Founded in 2016, Biohub aims to prevent and cure diseases through the creation of a “high-accuracy predictive model of the cell” that researchers can use to carry out simulations. To support this effort, the US Department of Energy will invest more than $500 million over the next five years, while the National Institutes of Health will contribute datasets, repositories, and knowledge bases stemming from previous federal investment totalling over $500 million. “An accurate predictive model of biology could dramatically accelerate scientific discovery by enabling scientists to perform experiments digitally,” Alex Rives, Biohub’s head of science, says in the press release. “The creation of a virtual cell is one of the most important challenges for the next era of science. It will require coordinated data generation efforts at a national and international scale, which is why these partners are coming together.” Update, October 7th: Clarified that Google, Meta, and Isomorphic Labs are investing in Biohub’s Virtual Biology initiative.

articles.title: SpaceX alumni nab $100M to rethink shipping with autonomous freight trains | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Parallel Systems raised $100 million to scale production of its autonomous electric rail vehicle, which can shuttle thousands of pounds of freight up to 500 miles.
articles.body:
The railroad industry was one of the first to disrupt how the world worked with technology, but lately, innovation in freight railroading has amounted to little more than longer and longer trains.

That has led many railroads to abandon shorter routes, ceding a chunk of the $1 trillion surface freight market to trucking companies. But as diesel prices reach record highs, some of those very trucking companies are going bust, leaving a hole in the market. Recently, at least 16 trucking companies went bankrupt over only a few weeks.

Parallel Systems might have a way to keep freight moving while allowing railroads to recapture market share. The startup has developed a rail vehicle capable of moving over several tons of freight as far as 500 miles without an operator. If the company can scale production of its Panther vehicles, it stands to make railroads profitable over short hauls once again.

“Less than 500 miles is hard for railroads to do competitively,” Matt Soule, co-founder and CEO of Parallel Systems, told TechCrunch. “Our technology allows them to take some of that trucking, and it’s for the public’s benefit.”

Because it runs on railroads, Parallel’s vehicle doesn’t contribute to traffic congestion, and because it’s battery powered, it doesn’t pollute. To scale manufacturing of its third-generation vehicle and speed the commercial rollout, Parallel Systems has raised a $100 million Series C led by AVP, with participation from Hillspire, Agility Global, Cobalt Capital, Anthos Capital, Congruent Ventures, Riot Ventures, and Collaborative Fund.

Soule and his co-founders started Parallel Systems in 2020 after years at SpaceX, where they designed rocket avionics systems.

Parallel’s vehicles can travel either independently or in platoons, which tend to be shorter than typical trains. It’s an approach that bucks the prevailing strategy used by railroads, known as precision railroading: As the railroad industry has matured, investor pressure has driven companies to build longer trains and operate them on fixed schedules, which helps spread some costs like labor across more freight.

As railroads have pulled back from smaller routes, trucking companies have stepped in. Today, some 60% of freight trips in the U.S. are under 500 miles, and trucking companies handle a majority of those.

But more trucks on the road means more congestion, and nowhere is that more apparent than at ports. “If you ever go to the Port of Savannah, you see the truck lines coming in and out of the port — it’s insanity,” Soule said.

Unlike traditional train cars, Parallel’s vehicles don’t have couplers, instead forming uncoupled platoons that move down the rails. The coupler-free design means that, once a platoon reaches a train yard, the vehicles can split up without needing human intervention. And after the Panther is cleared to operate on a section of track, its sensors monitor the rails to ensure the track ahead is clear of obstacles.

Trucking companies have been intrigued by Parallel, despite the fact that the startup is claiming part of a business they currently own. Drayage companies, which move freight short distances, make money for each load they deliver, but they don’t get to charge more when a truck gets stuck in a traffic jam, even at a port where such congestion is common. By moving freight closer to a customer’s door, Parallel allows trucking companies to make more deliveries per day. “They want certainty, they want to be able to move,” Soule said.

Parallel obtained approval a year and a half ago from the Federal Railroad Administration to operate near the Port of Savannah in Georgia, where it has been operating on 160 miles of track to prove the safety of its system.

“We’ve been verifying all the safety controls and operating practices that are best evaluated in a real-world setting with a path toward our first commercial payload coming up very soon,” Soule said.

articles.title: The scariest thing about gray-market peptides is how little we know
articles.summary: This week on Optimizer, a preprint study on real-world BPC-157 usage raises more questions than it can answer.
articles.body: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here. Finding concrete data about gray-market peptides is a Sisyphean task. Unlike bona fide clinical drug trials, there are no official numbers. There’s little to no safety data. Some peptides have more anecdotal evidence than others, but a stranger on r/peptides is, perhaps, not an ideal information source. The fact is most people partaking in a dubiously legal activity aren’t going to shout it from the rooftops. What we do know about many of these unregulated, unapproved substances is simply this: A lot of people are taking them, unsupervised by medical professionals. Take BPC-157 — one half of the infamous “Wolverine” stack. The BPC in BPC-157 stands for “body protection compound.” The substance was originally found in gastric juice in 1993 and is thought to promote injury recovery. It supposedly works by creating new blood vessels, promoting cell growth, and repairing damaged tissues like tendons, muscles, and ligaments. You know, Wolverine-y stuff. Sounds great. Except it’s not approved by any regulatory body, has primarily been studied in animals, and has limited clinical evidence in humans. One systematic review from 2025 found only 35 preclinical studies and a single clinical study for BPC-157 in humans. Nevertheless, BPC-157 is on a lot of people’s minds. That same systematic review states that, in 2024, there were over 50 million views for BPC-157 videos on YouTube and TikTok. According to Google Trends, there’s been a 1,600 percent increase in traditional web searches for BPC-157 in the United States in the last five years. That jumps to over 5,000 percent for YouTube searches. As for real-life usage data — it’s impossible to find reliable numbers. That said, a recent preprint study attempted to capture how real-world BPC-157 use has increased. The study, yet to go through peer review, is a retrospective look at anonymized electronic health records using a large language model to detect mentions of the peptide in clinical notes. This itself is an imperfect method, as BPC-157 has no insurance code or a uniform way for medical providers to indicate a patient is using it. Even so, the preprint highlights interesting — and concerning — trends. “[BPC-157 usage] was kind of benign during the pandemic and the deep end of the pandemic, but it’s skyrocketed over the last few quarters. Over the last three years, the use has increased significantly,” says Venky Soundararajan, one of the study’s authors and chief scientific officer of nference, an AI startup that uses LLMs to find insights from clinical records. Put plainly, the study found roughly 54 confirmed patients using BPC-157 in Q1 2022. (The real number is likely much higher, but this is a snapshot based on the records the researchers had access to.) That number jumped to 1,018 in Q1 2026. According to Soundararajan, about 33 percent of patients who used BPC-157 didn’t pursue any other therapies or drug use. Roughly half, however, stacked it with other substances. (Chief among those were testosterone, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and TB-500, the other half of the Wolverine stack, which also supports tissue repair.) He also noted that the majority of patients were taking BPC-157 orally, followed by injections. [Image: There’s a marked increased in BPC-157 usage. “The average BPC-157 user who’s showing up to the doctor is getting younger and younger — they’re in the upper 40s as an average age and is very likely a Caucasian white patient,” says Soundararajan. “And from the time the product is [first] used and the time they show up to discuss their use with a doctor, at least two months has elapsed.” As for the type of doctors, BPC-157 is most commonly reported to family practice and internal medicine, followed by gastroenterologists and orthopedic surgeons. Even so, this data has flaws, acknowledges Soundararajan. For example, he pointed out that 96 percent of patients who disclosed their usage were Caucasian, compared to the 2 percent that were African American. That’s a dramatic gap from what the researchers would’ve expected statistically based on the source data, which was 78 percent Caucasian and 17 percent African American. This doesn’t mean African Americans aren’t taking BPC-157 — they may simply feel less confident talking about it with doctors compared to Caucasians. As for why someone might feel that way, I’ve conducted interviews with peptide users who say they don’t want judgment, don’t trust their doctor is knowledgeable about the subject, or fear it may lead to repercussions with insurance. Another problem, Soundararajan says, is that this preprint can’t really give reliable insights as to BPC-157’s efficacy in humans or safety. Only a small subset reported adverse reactions — roughly 2 to 3 percent. However, the problem is that data is anecdotal. In a clinical setting, he explains, researchers and doctors evaluate adverse reactions on a graded scale. Minor, manageable adverse effects might get reported in records, but severe cases requiring hospitalizations may not. Pain, he says, is also not an objective assessment. In the study, most of the positive effects of BPC-157 were self-reported by patients. However, physicians rarely intervened to say they also saw an improvement in the patient’s condition. Also, 66 percent of the cases showed no documented response on whether BPC-157 worked or not — only that the patient had tried it. “The medical record has a bias. Obviously, there are those who are using the product for performance enhancement who are not talking about it,” says Soundararajan. For example, the top recorded reason for BPC-157 use is pain management. On the one hand, that indicates BPC-157 users may be turning to the substance because there’s an unmet need that legal therapies can’t address. But, he says, those are self-selecting patients. It’s possible that only patients with positive experiences were likely to talk about their usage in an official setting. Pro-peptide users might say this is evidence that BPC-157 works. Some might even conclude from this preprint that, given their individual circumstances, the risk calculus is worth a go. But from a regulatory standpoint, this simply isn’t good enough. [Image: Again, this shows part of a picture, but not the whole. Perhaps the scariest thing is that even Soundararajan can’t say whether the preprint truly says anything about BPC-157. The patients in the preprint obtained the peptide from gray-market sources, so it’s possible that some were taking another substance entirely. There’s always the chance that the positive effects recorded are simply the placebo effect. We’ll never know. But this is the sort of information physicians, researchers, journalists, regulators, and the peptide-curious have to go off of. A fuzzy picture that tells part of a story, but not the entirety. Imperfect data like this is better than nothing, but it raises more questions than it half-answers. The only thing that anyone can truly conclude from a study like this? We don’t know enough, but BPC-157 isn’t going away anytime soon. Doctors will have to start thinking about how to talk to patients who do turn to the gray market. “The reason we are handicapped, not only us but others when they try to replicate these studies, is that they’ll be relying on clinical notes alone,” says Soundararajan. “You need to make it easy for the healthcare provider to structure the conversations that they’re having with patients for unapproved products. This is one thing where we think regulation should change. We believe health record manufacturers need to make it easy for doctors to record. Who’s the source? Where did you get the product from?” Even if that helps paint a clearer picture of gray-market use, that, too, is a stopgap solution. One thing that everyone can agree on is that both prospective studies and gold-standard clinical trials are necessary. It’s “just” a matter of who will pony up the millions required. And it’s not isolated to BPC-157. This goes for all the commonly used gray-market peptides. Until then, incomplete data is all we have.

articles.title: In 2010, conservationists began releasing captive-bred wētāpunga after the species survived naturally on one island; 15 years and 11,000 releases later, four generations are established on two islands
articles.summary: After decades of decline, New Zealand's largest giant wētā, the wētāpunga, is showing signs of recovery with successful captive breeding and releases leading to four established generations on two islands.
articles.body: A giant insect that can grow to nearly 10cm and weigh as much as a mouse is showing signs of recovery after decades of decline.The wētāpunga, New Zealand’s largest giant wētā species, was once found across parts of the North Island but disappeared from the mainland after habitat loss and introduced predators drove its numbers down.According to the Department of Conservation (DOC), the species’ decline began after early European settlers cleared large areas of land for farming, destroying much of the wētāpunga's habitat. Introduced rats, stoats and other pests added further pressure, causing populations to fall dramatically and eventually disappear from all areas except Te Hauturu-o-Toi, also known as Little Barrier Island.By the 1990s, the species was considered endangered. With the remaining population too small for direct translocations, conservationists developed a captive breeding programme to increase its numbers before releasing the insects into suitable habitats.Breeding programme beginsThe programme began with a small number of wētāpunga collected from Little Barrier Island and taken to Butterfly Creek, where conservationists worked on developing reliable breeding methods.The first captive-bred insects were released on Motuora Island in 2010 and Tiritiri Matangi Island in 2011. Auckland Zoo established a second breeding colony in 2012, helping researchers refine methods for raising the insects.Young wētāpunga nymphs are fed fresh foliage and leaf litter, along with fish-flake protein. The additional protein is particularly important during the earliest stages of their development.Over the past 15 years, conservation teams have carried out 45 translocations involving more than 11,000 wētāpunga. The insects have been released at 10 new sites, including predator-free islands and fenced mainland reserves.Four generations born in the wildThe releases are now showing signs of longer-term success.At least four generations of wētāpunga have been born in the wild on Motuora and Tiritiri Matangi. The presence of multiple generations indicates that populations are reproducing without relying solely on continued releases from captive breeding facilities.The species' conservation status has also improved. It was classified as “Threatened Nationally Endangered” in 2004 but was listed as “Threatened Nationally Increasing” in 2022.Community restoration groups have also played a role by raising funds, helping organise releases and monitoring the insects after they were returned to the wild.Ngāti Manuhiri, the kaitiaki and mana whenua of Little Barrier Island, has supported the programme. The iwi regards the wētāpunga as a taonga species.One of the world’s largest insectsThe wētāpunga is the largest species of giant wētā and the heaviest orthopteran in the world.Females can weigh about as much as a mouse, while their bodies can reach around 10cm in length. Their legs can give them a span of roughly 20cm.Despite their size, the insects remain vulnerable to predators and habitat changes. Their disappearance from mainland areas illustrates the impact introduced species can have on native insects that evolved without such predators.The conservation programme has therefore focused not only on increasing numbers but also on establishing populations in places where the insects can survive and reproduce.Methods could help other threatened insectsChris Green, an honorary research associate at New Zealand’s Department of Conservation and co-author of the study, said the future of the wētāpunga looks promising. The researchers documented the breeding and release programme in a study published in the New Zealand Journal of Zoology, noting that the methods could also provide useful information for conserving other threatened invertebrates.Green described the scale of the programme, involving more than 11,000 releases, as extraordinary.The breeding techniques are already being used to inform conservation work involving the Māhoenui giant wētā at Ōtorohanga Kiwi House. The knowledge could also benefit conservation efforts for species such as the Canterbury knobbled weevil and native stag beetles.The programme has expanded the wētāpunga's presence beyond the single island population that remained in the wild. Continued monitoring will help determine whether the newly established populations remain self-sustaining.

articles.title: Noah’s Ark mystery deepens as archaeologists drill into Turkey’s Mount Ararat site for first time, collect soil samples from depths of up to 60 feet to search for evidence of ancient wood
articles.summary: The long-running Noah’s Ark mystery has taken a new turn after researchers drilled into the Durupinar formation, a boat-shaped geological site near Mount
articles.body: The long-running Noah’s Ark mystery has taken a new turn after researchers drilled into the Durupinar formation, a boat-shaped geological site near Mount Ararat in eastern Turkey.The formation has attracted researchers and Noah’s Ark enthusiasts since its identification in 1959. The latest fieldwork involved around 20 researchers from five countries, who collected hundreds of soil samples from both inside and outside the formation.Some of the samples were taken from depths of approximately 60 feet as researchers attempted to determine whether the site contains evidence of human activity or decaying wood.Andrew Jones, vice president of the Noah's Ark Research Project, said the team did not encounter a solid mass of limestone or other rock while drilling."We were hitting mainly soil," Jones said, according to Fox News. He added that the findings could challenge claims that the entire formation is simply a natural rock structure.Researchers find higher organic matter inside formationOne of the most intriguing findings from the Mount Ararat Noah’s Ark search involves carbon levels in the soil.Researchers said samples collected from within the Durupinar formation contained carbon levels roughly 40% higher than samples taken outside it. According to the team, the difference could potentially be associated with a higher concentration of organic material, including wood.However, the researchers have not established that the organic material comes from an ancient wooden vessel.The samples collected during the 2026 field season are now expected to undergo further laboratory analysis over the winter. Researchers say those results will be crucial in determining whether the site contains evidence that could explain its unusual structure.Pottery fragments found near Noah’s Ark siteThe international research team also discovered pottery fragments in the broader area surrounding the formation.The pottery could date to a period potentially relevant to the traditional Noah’s Ark timeline, although researchers stressed that none of the pottery fragments were found inside the Durupinar formation itself.Jones suggested that the discoveries could be connected to ancient settlements that once existed near the site."You can connect the dots," Jones said. "If this is Noah's Ark, we have people living right beside it."The pottery therefore provides an additional archaeological question but does not, by itself, establish a connection between the formation and the Biblical ark.What does the Bible say about Noah’s Ark?According to the Biblical account in Genesis, Noah’s Ark was built by Noah to protect his family and pairs of animals from a catastrophic flood.The Biblical story says the floodwaters covered the Earth before eventually receding. The possibility that the ark came to rest somewhere in the region of Mount Ararat has inspired centuries of speculation and exploration.The Durupinar formation has consequently become one of the most closely watched potential Noah’s Ark sites, despite continuing scientific debate over its origin.Earlier study called Durupinar a natural formationThe latest investigation comes amid decades of skepticism surrounding the site.A 1996 study published in the Journal of Geoscience Education examined the formation and concluded that it was naturally occurring.That conclusion remains important context for the current Noah’s Ark research. The new drilling project has not established that the Durupinar formation is Noah's Ark, and the researchers themselves say the investigation is not complete."What excites me most is that questions debated for decades can now be investigated using physical samples from documented locations and depths," Jones told Newsweek. "We have taken a substantial step forward in our ability to test the site, not completed the investigation."Noah’s Ark evidence remains unconfirmedDespite the renewed attention surrounding the Mount Ararat Noah’s Ark discovery, researchers have not confirmed that the Durupinar formation is the Biblical ark.The elevated organic matter, soil composition and nearby pottery fragments are clues that require additional analysis rather than definitive proof.Jones also acknowledged the skepticism surrounding the project, joking that some people view the search as being as unlikely as looking for "Santa's house."For now, the Noah’s Ark mystery remains unresolved. The laboratory analysis of the 2026 soil samples could provide researchers with more information about the history of the Durupinar formation, but whether those results establish a connection to Noah’s Ark remains an open question.

articles.title: Wild blacktip sharks can hear sounds from nearly 250 feet away and pinpoint where they come from; Florida experiments reveal how the predators locate sound underwater
articles.summary: Wild blacktip sharks may have a more sophisticated sense of hearing than scientists previously realised.
articles.body: Wild blacktip sharks may have a more sophisticated sense of hearing than scientists previously realised. A study by researchers at Florida Atlantic University found that free-swimming sharks can detect low-frequency sounds from as far as 74 metres, or roughly 243 feet, away and respond by turning sharply away from the source. The findings were reported by ScienceDaily and Florida Atlantic University, with the research published in Integrative Organismal Biology. Scroll down to read more...Sharks hear more than scientists could previously measureSound is particularly important underwater, where visibility can quickly become limited. For a predator such as the blacktip shark (Carcharhinus limbatus), noises and vibrations travelling through the water could provide information about prey, predators or other animals long before they become visible. Scientists already knew that sharks respond to low-frequency sounds. What had remained unclear was how far a wild shark could detect such a signal and whether it could determine its direction.The new research provides one of the clearest field measurements yet. Researchers studied wild blacktip sharks in the clear, shallow waters off southeastern Florida. Rather than testing captive animals, the team observed sharks swimming freely in their natural environment, allowing them to examine hearing behaviour under more realistic conditions.An underwater speaker became the testTo investigate the sharks’ response, scientists placed an underwater speaker in the water and played controlled, low-frequency sounds. At the same time, an aerial drone recorded the movements of sharks from above. The sounds were tested across several frequency ranges, including 100–200 Hz, 200–400 Hz and 400–800 Hz. The researchers also used a much higher-frequency sound as a control.The sharks responded to the tested low-frequency signals from distances of at least 62 metres. Some responses occurred at approximately 74 metres, demonstrating that the animals could react to sounds well beyond the acoustic near field, where scientists had previously expected their ability to detect sound to be strongest.The sharks did more than simply reactOne of the most interesting observations was the direction of the sharks’ movements. When they detected the sound, the animals made sudden turns ranging from about 20 to 160 degrees and then rapidly moved away from the speaker. That consistent directional response gave researchers evidence that the sharks were not merely detecting that a sound existed. They could determine where it was coming from.Across 209 recorded responses, 71.6% occurred in the acoustic far field. The sharks also failed to respond to the high-frequency control sound, despite it being played at a comparable volume. That distinction matters because it challenges the idea that sharks’ ability to orient toward underwater sounds is restricted to the immediate vicinity of a sound source.Why directional hearing matters underwaterThe ability to detect a distant sound and determine its direction could be valuable in an environment where vision is often unreliable. A sound travelling through the ocean can carry information well beyond the distance at which a shark could visually identify another animal. Detecting such signals could therefore give a shark additional time to investigate a potential food source or move away from a possible threat.The study does not show that blacktip sharks use sound alone to hunt or navigate. Instead, it demonstrates that acoustic information can trigger a strong directional response at surprisingly long distances. For researchers, that opens a wider question about how sharks combine hearing with their other highly developed senses.A new look at the shark’s acoustic worldThe findings are particularly significant because they come from sharks behaving freely in the ocean rather than animals tested in laboratory tanks. Observing the animals from above with a drone allowed researchers to measure changes in swimming direction without interfering with their movement.The work also adds to a growing understanding of how marine predators perceive an environment in which sound can travel farther and more reliably than many visual signals. For blacktip sharks, a faint underwater sound may therefore be much more informative than it appears to humans standing above the surface. What sounds like distant background noise to us could provide a shark with a directional clue from hundreds of feet away.

articles.title: Rassvet: por que Rússia tenta criar sua própria Starlink para a guerra na Ucrânia | G1
articles.standfirst: Após perder acesso clandestino à rede de Elon Musk, Moscou acelera projeto de satélites para comunicações militares e operação de drones. Sistema ainda enfrenta limitações técnicas, mas já preocupa autoridades ucranianas.
articles.summary: Moscou acelera desenvolvimento de rede própria de internet via satélite após perder acesso aos terminais da Starlink de Elon Musk. Tecnologia virou ativo estratégico na guerra.
articles.body:
Ucrânia afirma que a Rússia estaria acelerando a implantação da nova rede de internet via satélite — Foto: Adam88/Pond5 Images/IMAGO via DW

A Rússia está acelerando o desenvolvimento de sua própria rede de internet via satélite após sofrer um revés no campo de batalha na Ucrânia no início deste ano com a perda do acesso clandestino aos terminais da Starlink.

O serviço da empresa SpaceX , do bilionário Elon Musk , é conhecido por sua capacidade de prover acesso rápido e estável à internet em quase qualquer lugar do mundo. Amplamente utilizado pelas tropas ucranianas na guerra, ele é fundamental para a operação de drones e mísseis e a comunicação tática.

Isso porque, num campo de batalha moderno, é preciso enviar e receber grandes volumes de dados, como transmissões em vídeo de drones. E problemas de conectividade, ainda que durem segundos, podem fazer a diferença entre o sucesso e o fracasso de uma operação.

"A Starlink era tão importante que os russos tentaram durante muito tempo usá-la para seus próprios propósitos militares", afirma à DW Clayton Swope, diretor de defesa e segurança do Centro de Estudos Estratégicos e Internacionais (CSIS). "A Rússia não tinha nada que pudesse competir com isso."

É aí que entra a Rassvet (do russo "aurora"), aposta do Kremlin para reduzir sua dependência de tecnologias estrangeiras e obter capacidades semelhantes às oferecidas pela Starlink.

A rede alternativa é desenvolvida pela empresa russa aeroespacial Bureau 1440, e já preocupa autoridades ucranianas.

Por que a Rússia precisa tanto de alternativa à Starlink

A Starlink funciona como um provedor de internet baseado no espaço. Diferentemente dos sistemas tradicionais, que utilizam um número relativamente pequeno de satélites em órbitas elevadas, a rede da SpaceX opera milhares de satélites na órbita baixa da Terra.

Pequenos terminais em solo se conectam ao satélite que estiver passando sobre a região, permitindo acesso à internet mesmo quando torres de telefonia são destruídas, cabos de fibra óptica são cortados ou tropas operam em áreas remotas.

Como explica Swope, no início do conflito, a Ucrânia chegou a levar vantagem sobre a Rússia justamente porque tinha acesso à rede Starlink e a Rússia, não.

Satélites russos da Rassvet já estão em órbita

Soldado russo opera dispositivo de conexão na Ucrânia — Foto: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance via DW

No final de março, a Bureau 1440 levou a órbita seus primeiros 16 satélites de banda larga, capazes de prover conexão de até 1 gigabite por segundo. Hoje já são 31, e a meta é ter 292 deles em operação até 2027, segundo a Radio Free Europe.

Mas a capacidade dos satélites Rassvet é muito inferior à dos equipamentos mais modernos da SpaceX , como aponta o astrofísico e historiador espacial Jonathan McDowell.

"A atual geração da Starlink tem cerca de 100 gigabits por segundo. A próxima geração terá dez vezes mais do que isso. Até mesmo o sistema OneWeb, disponível na Europa, tem cerca de 10 gigabits por segundo. Portanto, o Rassvet está na extremidade inferior da capacidade desses sistemas de megaconstelações de internet por satélite", explica.

Além da capacidade inferior, o Rassvet também enfrenta desafios técnicos. Segundo o Instituto para o Estudo da Guerra (ISW), a primeira leva de satélites lançada em março atingiu a altitude prevista.

Já um segundo lançamento, realizado em julho, ficou abaixo do esperado, tendo alcançado entre 300 e 400 quilômetros de altitude.

Isso importa porque quanto mais alta a órbita de um satélite, maior é a área que ele é capaz de cobrir na Terra. E como eles ficam em movimento, cada aparelho só consegue prover uma pequena janela de conectividade sobre uma área determinada à medida que ele se desloca.

É por isso que são necessários vários satélites, muito mais dos que a Rússia dispõe agora, para obter uma boa cobertura.

Swope vê com ceticismo as ambições do Kremlin de criar sua própria Starlink. "A grande questão é se isso acontecerá. Nem sequer é quando", afirma.

Ele aponta que alguns satélites tiveram "falhas completas" e não estão "nas órbitas corretas esperadas". "Neste momento, a utilidade de um sistema como esse é muito pequena, oferecendo uma janela muito curta de cobertura apenas algumas vezes por dia sobre a Ucrânia", diz.

Além disso, a conectividade ainda dependerá de terminais, que terão de ser produzidos em larga escala pela Rússia, e de estruturas de controle operacional na Terra resilientes a ataques ucranianos.

Apesar das claras limitações do programa russo, McDowell avalia que a rede não precisa necessariamente igualar a Starlink para ter utilidade militar.

Segundo ele, mesmo uma infraestrutura menos avançada pode ajudar em comunicações militares e coordenação de drones no campo de batalha.

Soldado do serviço secreto ucraniano prepara drone para lançamento: sem internet ultraveloz, guerra seria outra — Foto: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo/picture alliance via DW

O vice-chefe da inteligência militar da Ucrânia, Vadym Skibitsky, alertou que a Rússia estaria acelerando a implantação da nova rede.

"Eles já começaram os lançamentos muito mais rapidamente do que o planejado originalmente. Por enquanto, o sistema só pode operar de forma intermitente, quando um satélite passa sobre nosso território. Quando a Rússia implantar uma constelação completa de satélites, o sistema funcionará como a Starlink. Já há discussões sobre como neutralizá-lo", afirmou.

Corrida global por alternativas à Starlink

A guerra na Ucrânia reforçou a percepção de que a internet via satélite se tornou um ativo estratégico.

A principal lição tirada por muitos governos do conflito é que é arriscado depender da infraestrutura de uma única empresa privada em cenários de conflito.

A China desenvolve suas próprias megaconstelações de satélites e estuda há anos as vantagens militares proporcionadas pela Starlink. A União Europeia investe bilhões no projeto Iris², uma rede soberana de comunicações via satélite. Já a Amazon trabalha no Projeto Kuiper, concorrente americano da Starlink.

Para Swope, a dependência global da SpaceX ainda é grande. "Existe hoje uma dependência global da SpaceX para lançamentos espaciais e para conectividade, como a Starlink. Há essencialmente apenas um concorrente neste momento. É uma empresa europeia, a OneWeb, que não tem nem de longe a capacidade da Starlink", afirma.

Diante desse cenário, a expansão de projetos como Rassvet, Iris² e Kuiper sugere o início de uma nova corrida espacial. Desta vez, o foco não é a exploração do espaço, mas o controle das comunicações globais e das capacidades militares associadas a elas.

articles.title: Margaret Hamilton: morre a engenheira que levou os EUA à Lua | G1
articles.standfirst: Considerada a pessoa mais importante no trabalho inovador de desenvolver um software para o programa lunar Apollo da Nasa, Margaret Hamilton faleceu aos 90 anos.
articles.summary: Margaret Hamilton, pioneira da engenharia de software da Nasa e líder da equipe que programou os computadores da missão Apollo, faleceu aos 90 anos.
articles.body:
Margaret Hamilton, aqui em foto de 1969, liderou um grupo que programou os computadores usados na missão de pouso na Lua da Nasa — Foto: AP Photo/picture alliance

A engenheira de software Margaret Hamilton, líder da equipe que programou os primeiros computadores usados pela missão Apollo da Nasa para levar humanos à Lua, morreu no dia 30 de setembro, aos 90 anos. A morte foi anunciada nesta quarta-feira (07) pelo Instituto de Tecnologia de Massachusetts (MIT), onde ela trabalhou de 1959 até meados da década de 1970.

A universidade a descreveu como alguém muito influente no setor de desenvolvimento de software, dizendo que ela "abriu novos caminhos na ciência da computação e na engenharia”.

O chefe da Nasa, Jared Isaacmen, prestou homenagem na rede social X, chamando Hamilton de "uma pioneira cujo trabalho ajudou a tornar a [missão] Apollo e as primeiras viagens do homem à Lua possível”.

Hamilton estudou matemática antes de se mudar para Boston, em Massachusetts, em 1959. Ela começou a trabalhar no MIT logo depois e, em 1965, se candidatou a uma vaga em um laboratório da universidade que estava procurando pessoas para desenvolver software para "levar um homem à Lua". O laboratório tinha ganhado um contrato da Nasa para construir o software de voo de bordo para o programa Apollo.

Contratada, a americana se tornou a primeira programadora do projeto, disse o MIT, acrescentando que ela também foi a primeira mulher a ocupar esse cargo no projeto. Inicialmente, ela trabalhou no primeiro software para as missões Apollo não tripuladas, antes de ser promovida para liderar a equipe que desenvolvia o software de voo de bordo para as missões tripuladas.

"Em 1968, ela já era diretora-assistente e responsável pela equipe do Módulo de Comando e Serviço [da Apollo], e mais de 400 pessoas trabalhavam no software da Apollo", disse o MIT. "Dizer que Margaret Hamilton foi uma pioneira, como dizer que ela estava à frente de seu tempo, seria um eufemismo e tanto", disse Olivier de Weck, professor do programa Apollo e chefe interino do Departamento de Aeronáutica e Astronáutica do MIT.

"Ela era engenheira de software numa época em que essa área ainda estava engatinhando, e não só desenvolveu códigos avançados sozinha, como também liderou uma equipe no uso dessa tecnologia incipiente, para criar um dos sistemas mais complexos que a humanidade já havia construído", acrescentou de Weck.

Em 2009, Hamilton disse ao MIT News, sobre o tempo em que trabalhou no programa Apollo, que "não havia segunda chance". "Nós sabíamos disso. Levávamos nosso trabalho a sério; muitos de nós começaram essa jornada ainda na casa dos 20 anos de idade."

"Encontrar soluções e novas ideias era uma aventura. Dedicação e comprometimento eram algo natural", acrescentou ela. "Como o software era um mistério, uma 'caixa preta', tínhamos total liberdade e confiança por parte do alto escalão do MIT." "Olhando para trás, éramos as pessoas mais sortudas do mundo; não tínhamos escolha a não ser: ser pioneiros."

Hamilton publicou mais de 130 artigos e fundou suas próprias empresas de software: a Higher Order Software e a Hamilton Technologies. Em 2016, ela recebeu a Medalha Presidencial da Liberdade, a maior honraria civil dos EUA, das mãos do então presidente Barack Obama, cuja menção honrosa dizia: "Hamilton definiu novas formas de engenharia de software e ajudou a lançar um setor que mudaria para sempre a história da humanidade. Sua arquitetura de software levou a avanços gigantescos para a humanidade, escrevendo o código que ajudou os Estados Unidos a pisar na Lua."

articles.title: Cientistas criam primeiros relógios nucleares do mundo | G1
articles.standfirst: Nova tecnologia usa o núcleo de átomos de tório para medir o tempo e pode, no futuro, superar a precisão dos relógios atômicos mais avançados.
articles.summary: Tecnologia usa o núcleo de átomos de tório para medir o tempo e pode, no futuro, superar a precisão dos relógios atômicos mais avançados.
articles.body:
Cristal de fluoreto de cálcio em um suporte com um feixe de laser sondando os núcleos de tório em laboratório da TU Wien, em Viena, Áustria 7 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: T. Schumm, TU Wien/Imagem cedida via REUTERS

Equipes científicas que trabalham separadamente em Viena e Pequim desenvolveram os dois primeiros relógios nucleares operacionais do mundo, em um importante avanço na medição do tempo, que promete amplas aplicações práticas e oferece uma nova ferramenta para investigar a física fundamental.

Os dois dispositivos representam a próxima geração de relógios atômicos, máquinas de medição de tempo ultraprecisas criadas pela primeira vez em 1949.

As duas equipes de pesquisa, ao descreverem suas conquistas nesta quarta-feira em artigos científicos publicados na revista Nature, afirmaram que os relógios nucleares têm o potencial de superar os melhores relógios atômicos convencionais, mas ainda não o fazem.

Eles são chamados de relógios nucleares não porque sejam movidos a fusão ou fissão nuclear, como um leigo poderia supor, mas porque o tempo é calculado a partir do monitoramento de como a luz -- um laser de alta potência -- interage com o núcleo de um átomo.

Ambos os relógios nucleares são baseados em uma forma, ou isótopo, do elemento tório, chamado tório-229, aprisionado em cristais de fluoreto de cálcio no estado sólido.

“As duas equipes trabalharam de forma independente e conseguiram colocar em funcionamento relógios nucleares de tório-229 ao mesmo tempo, utilizando abordagens experimentais diferentes. Acho isso muito encorajador, pois mostra que o conceito é robusto e não depende de uma implementação técnica específica”, disse o físico Shiqian Ding, da Universidade de Tsinghua, na China, que ajudou a liderar a equipe responsável pelo relógio de Pequim.

“A criação de um relógio nuclear era algo com que os físicos sonhavam há quase 50 anos. Na minha equipe, temos trabalhado nesse objetivo desde 2008”, disse o físico Thorsten Schumm, da TU Wien, na Áustria, que ajudou a liderar a equipe responsável pelo relógio de Viena.

Schumm prevê aplicações para os relógios nucleares em áreas como navegação por satélite, sincronização de transferência de dados, topografia e metrologia, que é o estudo da medição e de suas aplicações práticas.

Os relógios atômicos convencionais medem o tempo usando lasers ou micro-ondas para fazer com que partículas subatômicas chamadas elétrons saltem de um nível de energia para outro na camada de um átomo, utilizando elementos como o césio ou o estrôncio.

Os novos relógios nucleares medem o tempo usando lasers para fazer com que partículas subatômicas chamadas prótons e nêutrons saltem de um nível de energia para outro dentro do núcleo de um átomo, neste caso, o tório-229.

A ideia é que o monitoramento dessas transições dentro do núcleo atômico possa atingir níveis de precisão ainda maiores do que o monitoramento nos elétrons, pois um núcleo atômico é muito menor do que a camada que o circunda, onde residem os elétrons.

Schumm disse que o relógio nuclear ainda está “longe de seu desempenho almejado”, com os pesquisadores buscando aperfeiçoar a tecnologia.

“O que é realmente interessante aqui: o relógio de Viena possui cristais de tório ligeiramente melhores -- maior concentração, melhores propriedades ópticas --, enquanto a equipe de Pequim tem um laser mais potente. Assim, apenas reunindo esses componentes, já podemos construir um relógio significativamente melhor”, disse Schumm.

Os melhores relógios atômicos convencionais podem funcionar por bilhões de anos perdendo ou ganhando apenas um segundo.

Essa ultraprecisão tem sido vital para aplicações como sistemas globais de navegação por satélite e comunicações pela internet, celular e fibra óptica.

Os pesquisadores acreditam que os relógios nucleares, uma vez aperfeiçoados, podem desempenhar essa função ainda melhor e podem ser construídos de forma a serem menos volumosos e delicados.

Os relógios nucleares são promissores na investigação da física fundamental. A equipe de Viena demonstrou que seu relógio poderia realizar um experimento de física de precisão ao tentar detectar a matéria escura, componente crucial do cosmos que, até o momento, escapou à observação.

O experimento, na verdade, não detectou matéria escura, mas o relógio nuclear teve um desempenho comparável ao dos melhores relógios atômicos.

“Isso abre as portas para um universo físico totalmente novo”, disse Schumm.

articles.title: En 1974, Francia diseñó el Aérotrain: un tren flotante sin ruedas que superaba los 430 km/h y el gobierno dejó de apoyarlo por la crisis de petróleo
articles.standfirst: Apenas tuvo un año de desarrollo, pero fue capaz de llevar a 1.400 pasajeros
articles.summary: Apenas tuvo un año de desarrollo, pero fue capaz de llevar a 1.400 pasajeros
articles.body: A principios de la década de 1970, mucho antes de que los trenes de alta velocidad fuesen la norma en todos los países europeos, Francia experimentó con una tecnología futurista que, hoy en día, comienza a ser una realidad. Diseñado por el ingeniero Jean Bertin, el Aérotrain fue un vehículo pionero que prometía conectar ciudades a velocidades imposibles en la época, marcando un hito histórico el 5 de marzo de 1974 al alcanzar un récord de 430,4 km/h. La clave del Aérotrain era su revolucionario funcionamiento para aquellos años: desplazarse sin tocar el suelo. El vehículo operaba mediante un sistema de colchón de aire comprimido que elevaba la estructura unos milímetros por encima del trazado. Al eliminar por completo las ruedas metálicas y el contacto con la vía, se reducía la fricción mecánica y podía superar con facilidad los 400 km/h. Se construyó una pista exclusiva de hormigón con forma de T invertida, elevada a 10 metros de altura a lo largo de 18 kilómetros en la región del Loiret, entre Saran y Ruan, muy cerca de París, al sur de la capital. El tren utilizaba propulsión neumática impulsada por queroseno, funcionando durante unas 100 horas sin registrar fallos estructurales graves. Sin embargo, a pesar de su éxito, y de haber llevado a 1.400 pasajeros en sus pruebas, el programa fue cancelado a finales de 1974. La versión oficial achacó la decisión al impacto de la crisis del petróleo, ya se usaba un alto volumen de combustible. Sin embargo, el factor determinante fue que el gobierno francés optó por priorizar el desarrollo del TGV (la marca utilizada por la compañía de ferrocarriles nacional francesa SNCF para los servicios en las líneas de alta velocidad que opera en Francia).

articles.title: In 2013, Arizona’s rare leopard frogs were under threat from invasive bullfrogs, but by 2019 conservationists had expanded their recovery network from 7 sites to 19
articles.summary: The Arizona project began with a problem that was easy to see but difficult to solve.
articles.body: The Arizona project began with a problem that was easy to see but difficult to solve. American bullfrogs had established themselves in the Cienega Creek watershed, where they could prey on Chiricahua leopard frogs and carry the fungal disease chytridiomycosis. The response involved more than removing the invasive frogs. Managers also had to keep them from returning, improve water sources and give the threatened leopard frogs places where they could breed and move between populations. According to The Nature Conservancy blog, by 2019, the area used for Chiricahua leopard frog reintroduction had expanded from seven sites covering 42 square kilometres in 2013 to 19 sites across 84 square kilometres.How Cienega Creek conservationists tackled invasive bullfrogs and frog declineCienega Creek runs through southeastern Arizona, where mountain drainage meets semidesert grassland and riparian habitat. Much of the watershed is protected within the Las Cienegas National Conservation Area and the Cienega Creek Natural Preserve, but protection alone did not remove the pressures facing its amphibians.The creek supports several species of conservation concern, including the lowland leopard frog, the threatened Chiricahua leopard frog and the endangered Gila chub and Gila topminnow. Its relatively small and isolated aquatic system also gave conservation managers an advantage. Unlike larger, connected waterways where invasive species can be difficult to contain, Cienega Creek offered a more manageable setting for attempting bullfrog eradication.American bullfrogs had arrived in the watershed during the mid-1980s. Their presence created a particular problem for Chiricahua leopard frogs. Bullfrogs are associated with the disappearance of the native species in other areas, both through predation and through their ability to carry and spread chytrid fungus, a pathogen linked to amphibian declines around the world.Removing the bullfrogs was only the first stepThe FROG Conservation Project had worked in the watershed from 2010 to 2013, with the wider partnership continuing under the same name from 2014 through 2019. Its work combined invasive species control with habitat restoration, monitoring and the establishment of additional leopard frog populations.Bullfrogs were successfully eradicated from the Cienega Creek complex in 2013. That did not mean the threat had disappeared. A separate population could move in from surrounding areas, so conservationists created a buffer zone extending through Sonoita towards the Mustang Mountains. Starting in 2013, University of Arizona scientists checked stock tanks in this area each year and removed bullfrogs when they were found. Arizona Game and Fish Department biologists joined the monitoring effort in 2015, with help from the US Forest Service and the Appleton-Whittell Research Ranch.The removal work itself varied with the habitat and life stage of the frogs. US Fish and Wildlife Service reported, teams used draining, dip and seine nets and, for adult bullfrogs in complicated pools, shooting with .22-calibre rifles. Fine-mesh hoop traps were useful for catching tadpoles. The timing mattered too, with early-season removal of adults and juveniles intended to prevent breeding and dispersal later in the summer.Arizona restored ponds to create stronger habitat for leopard frogsRemoving a predator would have meant little if suitable habitat was unavailable. Some livestock water infrastructure was enhanced or converted so that it could provide permanent, drought-resistant water for native wildlife as well as working ranches.The project found that larger ponds tended to hold more frogs, giving their populations greater resilience when conditions changed. Permanent water was important in an arid landscape, while vegetation such as pondweed could provide cover and feeding areas for young leopard frogs. Maintained ponds supplied by pumps and wells could also continue providing habitat during dry periods.The project eventually set out practical recommendations for new leopard frog habitat. Ponds were advised to be larger than 0.1 acres, retain permanent water and contain plants such as pondweed and spikerush. A deeper central section could provide a refuge when seasonal drying occurred or when pond infrastructure failed. Regular checks were also recommended so managers could keep track of water conditions and frog populations.The reintroduction network expandedThe changes became visible in the distribution of Chiricahua leopard frogs. As reported by US Fish and Wildlife Service, partners raised and released 4,769 frogs at 10 new sites. In 2013, the reintroduction area contained seven breeding sites covering about 42 square kilometres. By 2019, it had expanded to 19 sites covering 84 square kilometres.The case study does not say that 19 sites were all actively breeding by 2019. It reports that Chiricahua leopard frogs were present at 24 sites across the wider management area at that point, including six that were active breeding sites. The 19-site figure refers to the expanded reintroduction area and is therefore better understood as a measure of the network's reach rather than a count of breeding populations alone.Frogs were also moving between sites. The project recorded an average straight-line movement of 7.43 kilometres, while one Chiricahua leopard frog travelled 15.13 kilometres, described in the case study as the longest documented movement for the species. Such movements helped form what conservationists call a metapopulation, with separate breeding groups linked by occasional dispersal.Disease added another obstacle for threatened leopard frogsBullfrogs were not the only obstacle. Chytrid fungus was detected in the project area in autumn 2013, when a substantial die-off of Chiricahua leopard frogs was observed at wildlife ponds. Monitoring suggested that disease effects varied according to habitat, temperature and season. Natural spring-fed sites appeared to offer better adult survival through winter than some constructed ponds when chytrid was causing problems.

articles.title: Beagle 2: How a British scientist used Britpop's Blur to reach Mars
articles.summary: Colin Pillinger died believing that Beagle 2 had not landed, and now his work is being celebrated around the UK.
articles.body:
A series of plaques has been unveiled across the UK to celebrate the country's first spacecraft to reach another planet.

Yet the mastermind behind Beagle 2 was never your typical rocket scientist.

With his mutton-chop sideburns, West Country accent and infectious enthusiasm, Professor Colin Pillinger persuaded politicians, pop stars and the public to support what had seemed impossible: a British mission to Mars.

For years the story of this maverick scientist was synonymous with ambitious British failure. So what changed to make it worthy of nationwide celebration ?

Pillinger was born in Kingswood near Bristol and completed his degree at Swansea University.

He gained international recognition for his lunar research before moving to Cambridge University, where he analysed meteorites found in Antarctica that were believed to have come from Mars.

By the 1980s, he had become one of the founders of the Planetary and Space Sciences Research Institute at The Open University in Milton Keynes.

It was here he conceived the idea of sending a lander, named Beagle 2 by his wife, to Mars, where it could study the red planet directly for signs of life.

Space exploration was dominated by international superpowers and agencies such as Nasa, which had the funding for such expensive work.

Britain had no dedicated space agency, so Pillinger proposed that Beagle 2 hitch a ride aboard Mars Express, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft already scheduled to travel to the planet.

When the ride was approved in 1999, the ESA did not guarantee funding or wider support for the project.

The scientist believed that capturing the public's imagination would help attract financial backing.

Pallab Ghosh, the BBC's science correspondent, recalled being sceptical when he was sent to meet a "bloke in Milton Keynes who is sending a spaceship to Mars".

Those doubts deepened when Pillinger placed a model of Beagle 2 on the lawn. According to Ghosh, it "did not look much like a spaceship".

On another occasion, Pillinger loaded a Beagle 2 replica into a supermarket trolley and wheeled it around The Open University's car park , demonstrating its compact size to cameras.

The footage was later ridiculed on Have I Got News for You, ensuring it reached an even wider audience.

Pillinger persuaded Britpop band Blur to compose a distinctive call-sign that Beagle 2 would transmit to Earth after landing.

Artist Damien Hirst created a spot painting to serve as a calibration target for the lander's onboard camera.

The project eventually won financial support from the UK government, academic institutions, industrial contractors and private sponsors.

Beagle 2 was reportedly built for about £50m; in comparison Nasa spent $25bn on the Apollo programme during the 1960s.

Mars Express launched on 2 June 2003 with Beagle 2 aboard; it was due to reach Mars on Christmas Day.

On Christmas Eve, excited scientists and celebrities gathered at The Open University's London headquarters.

Members of Blur drank mulled wine, singer Myleene Klass handed out jelly babies, and the crowd waited for Beagle 2 to confirm it had landed safely.

Pillinger and his team believed it had descended too quickly after being caught out by Martian atmospheric conditions.

Official inquiries by the government and ESA criticised the project's finances and management structure .

Supporters argued the project had brought industries together behind a single planetary mission.

Pillinger, undeterred, proposed a successor, Beagle 3, which ESA rejected in 2004.

In his 2010 autobiography, My Life on Mars, he recalled a builder stopping him in The Open University car park to shake his hand.

He wrote: "There's nobody in the UK I didn't reach."

Pillinger died in May 2014 after suffering a brain haemorrhage and falling into a coma.

Eight months later, high-resolution images captured by Nasa revealed something surprising.

Sitting in the red dust, just 5km from its intended landing site, was the largely intact Beagle 2 .

The images confirmed that much of its landing sequence had worked. Its parachutes and cushioning airbags had deployed as planned.

However, its petal-like solar panels had failed to open fully, trapping the antenna and preventing Beagle 2 from communicating.

For his son Nic Pillinger, the discovery meant an achievement that had been "on ice for many years" could finally take its rightful place in history.

Reflecting on the fact that his father died without knowing the mission succeeded, Nick added: "My dad always spoke of himself as being the frontman to the band that was behind this.

"It wasn't just a one-man project. It was a huge number of people working across different institutions coming together to make it happen."

articles.title: India rejects Elon Musk's claim of discrimination over Starlink launch | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Starlink is still awaiting security clearance before it can seek spectrum and begin commercial services in India.
articles.body:
India has rejected Elon Musk’s claim that Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet service, is being unfairly blocked from launching in the country. The pushback comes as SpaceX struggles to turn years of regulatory work and partnerships with India’s biggest telecom operators into a commercial launch in one of the world’s largest internet markets.

On Wednesday, Musk accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s launch in India to maintain what he called their “monopolistic chokehold” on the country, without identifying them or providing evidence for his claim. He called the alleged blocking a “crime against the people of India” and argued that Starlink could bring affordable, high-speed internet to people who lack internet access.

Hours later, India’s Ministry of Communications pushed back , saying its regulatory framework for satellite communications is “fair and non-discriminatory.” The ministry said in a statement that Starlink and two other licensed satellite operators are all at “broadly the same regulatory stage.” It added that all three companies are undergoing security assessments that must be completed before they can seek spectrum, the radio frequencies that satellites use to send signal.

Starlink has spent over five years trying to enter India, a market with more than a billion internet subscribers. But it has yet to begin commercial services despite securing key regulatory approvals and partnering with telecom giants Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel last year. SpaceX has also set up a local team as it prepares for a launch, appointing former Payoneer executive Prabhakar Jayakumar to lead its India operations in December.

Musk’s comments came hours after Lauren Dreyer, Starlink’s vice president of business operations, appeared at a telecom industry conference, India Mobile Congress, in New Delhi and reiterated the company’s commitment to the market. “We stand ready to serve India,” Dreyer said, adding that Starlink wants to help realize Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s goal of achieving universal connectivity across the country.

Starlink said it already has more than 20 gateway sites (the ground stations that link its satellites to the internet) and hundreds of antennas on the ground in India, and has adapted its operations to meet the country’s regulatory, security, and data-sovereignty requirements. Moreover, SpaceX has positioned its satellite network as a complement to — rather than a replacement for — India’s terrestrial telecom networks.

SpaceX first attempted to launch Starlink in India in 2021. The company, however, had to refund preorders for its equipment in early 2022 after the Indian government called it out for “booking/rendering the satellite internet service” before getting the necessary licenses.

Starlink has also previously clashed with India’s largest telecom operators over how satellite spectrum should be allocated. Starlink pushed for spectrum to be assigned administratively, while Reliance Jio argued that it should be auctioned — a position that could have made Starlink’s entry more expensive. India ultimately sided with Starlink’s preferred approach , deciding to allocate satellite spectrum administratively rather than through an auction.

Jio and Airtel, the two biggest Indian telcos, are also pursuing their own satellite internet services , even as they have agreed to distribute Starlink in India. Jio is working with satellite operator SES on satellite broadband, while Airtel is a major backer of Eutelsat OneWeb, another licensed satellite operator in India.

While the timing of Starlink’s India launch remains unclear, the company launched Starlink Mobile, which connects ordinary phones to satellites, in neighboring Bangladesh this week .

Starlink, India’s Ministry of Communications, Reliance Jio, and Bharti Airtel did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos calls Mars a destination for humans, but wants to take Americans to Moon first, and in less than three years, as ...
articles.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has outlined an ambitious vision for the future of space exploration, arguing that while Mars remains a long-term destination
articles.body: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has outlined an ambitious vision for the future of space exploration, arguing that while Mars remains a long-term destination for humanity, the United States should focus on returning humans to the Moon first and establishing a permanent presence there. Speaking in an interview with Bret Baier on Fox News' "Special Report", the Amazon founder and Blue Origin executive chairman said the US must win the race against China to put humans back on the Moon. He expressed confidence that an American crewed lunar landing could happen by 2028, less than three years from now. "We have to beat China to the moon, and I believe we will beat China to the moon," Bezos said, adding that NASA and Blue Origin are working toward that goal.'We'll go to Mars, but we need to go to the Moon first'While Mars is often viewed as the next frontier for human exploration, Bezos said skipping the Moon would be a mistake. He described Earth's natural satellite as "a gift" because of its proximity and potential resources that could support deeper space missions. "We'll go to Mars. We'll do all the other things. But we need to go to the moon first," Bezos said during the interview. According to Bezos, establishing a sustainable lunar base could provide critical infrastructure for future exploration. He said routine cargo missions would be required to support a long-term human presence on the Moon, rather than treating lunar landings as one-off missions.Bezos argued that the Moon's resources could eventually play a significant role in supporting space development. He noted that lunar soil could potentially be used to manufacture solar cells, while oxygen produced on the Moon could serve as rocket propellant for missions travelling deeper into the solar system. "It won't just be a mission and leave," Bezos said. "It'll be a real sustainable lunar base."Jeff Bezos said Blue Origin plans to return its New Glenn rocketBezos said Blue Origin plans to return its New Glenn rocket to flight in December, after an explosion during an engine test in May that Baier raised during the broadcast. The next flight will carry Blue Ring, a vehicle designed to move payloads into different orbits and farther into space, he said. He praised the team for repairing the launch pad.Asked about plans to raise launches from one pad from 12 to 50 a year, he said Blue Origin is building three more pads. His long-term target is far bigger: fly daily, then hourly, then every minute. He acknowledged that his own team thinks he is crazy, but said he has seen "crazy things" come true before.He said he has personally invested $28 billion in Blue Origin, which recently raised $10 billion from outside investors for the first time. He said an IPO could come several years from now.Data centers in spaceOn the debate over data centers and electricity costs, Bezos pointed to Blue Origin's Project Sunrise. He said the company has applied to the Federal Communications Commission to launch more than 50,000 satellites that would act as orbital data centers, adding that there are good reasons to do so.AI and workBezos predicted AI would deliver double-digit productivity gains across the economy. He said some families might get by on one income or a three-day workweek, and that this could make hiring harder as people choose to work less. Baier challenged him by citing the roughly 30,000 corporate roles Amazon has cut since late last year. Bezos said Amazon was in a "very special position" because it expanded its workforce substantially during the pandemic.At Prometheus, the startup where he is co-founder and co-CEO, Bezos said the goal is an "artificial general engineer" that helps people turn ideas into physical products. Asked whether AI is a bubble, he said it is very hard to know, but argued that the inventions survive even if the bubble bursts, as fiber-optic cable did after the internet boom. He urged a light regulatory touch while the technology is young, saying rules should target harmful uses rather than the technology itself.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
